16.5GOV-05 The Pre-Concept Gate and Ceiling on Conceptual Validity ​

In briefFirst explain what you actually observed, then decide whether a broad concept can explain it. Giving people one name does not prove they form one structural domain. Even when a concept fits, it cannot slide directly into deciding for others.

The framework must not force something into the category of “structural domain” and then use its own concept to prove that classification. Before formal mapping, answer in plain language. Can the parts be observed together? Is there a minimum boundary? Do actions within it repeatedly affect one another? Is there a shared problem, direction, risk, or constraint? Who bears the costs of maintaining it? Can results or bad news change subsequent practice?

If the pre-concept gate fails, the output is limited to describing phenomena, registering risks, or analyzing narratives. Even after it passes, the concept may be used at only one of five levels of strength.

Expressive level. Helps only to state feelings or similarities clearly.

Exploratory level. Can generate only questions and signals to observe.

Diagnostic level. External observable material permits judgments with low to moderate confidence.

Strong-judgment level. The object, evidence, scale, responsibility, and observation checks have all passed.

Action level. Requires external review, appeal, anti-retaliation, compensation, and withdrawal in addition to normative choice under Part 14, J authorization, and O procedures.

16.5Note

Understanding this section

16.5 GOV-05 Pre-conceptual Gate and Ceiling on Conceptual Validity

First explain what you actually observed, then decide whether a broad concept can explain it. Giving people one name does not prove they form one structural domain. Even when a concept fits, it cannot slide directly into deciding for others.

The pre-conceptual gate prevents circular reasoning: labeling an object with structural-domain vocabulary, then treating that label as evidence that the object really is a structural domain. Before formal mapping, explain whether the object can be observed jointly, where its minimum boundary lies, whether internal actions repeatedly affect one another, whether there is a shared problem, direction, risk, or constraint, who bears maintenance costs, and whether outcomes or bad news can change subsequent practices. Plain language does not imply absence of theoretical background. It requires making the proposed objects, relationships, and facts checkable without prior acceptance of this framework.

“Observable jointly” does not merely mean fitting into a column in one table, and a “minimum boundary” need not mean closure without exchange. Labeling all people in blue clothes together creates a classification, not proof of repeated mutual influence. Conversely, repair collaboration across locations may have verifiable links through tasks, tools, responsibilities, and risks without sharing enclosing walls. Shared problems, directions, risks, or constraints are different connections listed by the source; do not arbitrarily require unanimous views or one central will. Maintenance costs also require asking who bears unpaid work, waiting, or exposure, rather than observing only the nominal organizational leader.

The final question specifically checks whether bad news can change subsequent practice. Receiving information, issuing receipts, and collecting data do not mean information can influence later action; this connects to the distinctions among feedback, learning, and repair. Conversely, change does not establish successful repair, and one adjustment does not prove full structural-domain qualification. The pre-conceptual gate is a minimum review for entering formal mapping, not a few questions that complete all causal, value, and power judgments at once.

If the gate is not passed, the source permits phenomenon description, risk registration, and narrative analysis; indications of harm, local facts, or questions requiring observation can still be stated. The limit concerns how strongly material may be formally mapped into framework objects, not a prohibition on independent professional research. Those experiencing a situation do not need to prove a structural domain before they may describe it. If material is insufficient, specify the missing connection, boundary, or response evidence; distinguish actual contrary material from insufficient observation.

After the gate passes, five strengths of concept use remain. Expressive use helps articulate feelings or similarity without claiming an identified mechanism. Exploratory use turns intuitions into questions and observation signals without posing as diagnosis. Diagnostic use has externally observable material and permits low-to-moderate-confidence judgments, while still specifying objects and possible misjudgments. Strong judgment requires passing the object, evidence, scale, responsibility, and observation gates; confident tone or numerous evidence files alone cannot upgrade it. This section supplies no formula converting the five levels to percentages and does not claim that any domain material necessarily leads upward.

The action level additionally requires external review, appeals, protection against retaliation, compensation, and withdrawal, as well as Part Fourteen's normative choice, J authorization, and O procedures. Switching accounts for self-review cannot replace external review; appeals cannot be merely a mailbox; withdrawal cannot merely delete a report while leaving consequences untouched. Even a strong factual judgment still requires separate grounds for a reasonable target, who may decide, and what procedures permit execution. Concept-use ceilings must be assessed together with current use and evidence. The same material can support a low-strength observation without supporting a different high-impact action.

The strongest objection is that the pre-conceptual gate may exclude genuinely harmful but difficult-to-observe relationships. Vocabulary proficiency cannot resolve this risk. Preserve phenomenon and risk material, investigate why observation is difficult, and allow appropriate professional methods and low-exposure expression while preventing premature whole-object diagnosis. Conversely, relaxing the gate until any similarity passes would make concepts incapable of failure. A workable approach states what external material answers each question, what remains unknown, and the maximum currently supportable level, allowing contraction or upgrade when new facts appear.

The five strengths here are ceilings on concept use, not levels of human worth, institutional rankings, or aliases for the S0–S6 state prototypes in Part Eight §8.3. The diagram's order shows increasing evidential and protective obligations, not automatic real-world growth through stages. Professional classification examples can illustrate that naming requires conditions and scope, but astronomy's use of classification does not turn celestial bodies into personified governance subjects bearing responsibilities and appeals. Cross-domain analogy must stop at the small step it supports.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First describe the object, boundary, repeated influence, shared conditions, costs, and consequences of bad news without structural-domain labels.

  2. 2

    Check the external material needed for these questions; record unknowns or failures, avoiding concepts used to prove themselves.

  3. 3

    When the gate is not passed, retain descriptive, risk, and narrative responsibilities while stopping unsupported formal mapping.

  4. 4

    Even after passing, set the expressive, exploratory, diagnostic, or strong-judgment ceiling by evidence and use; labels do not permit direct jumps.

  5. 5

    For action, separately check normative choice, J permissions, O procedures, and review, appeal, and other protections; insufficient conditions preclude executing high-impact judgments.

Distinctions to keep clear

Can share a name

Objects fall under the same classification label.

≠

Has a verifiable shared structure

Actual material supports boundaries, repeated influence, shared conditions, maintenance costs, and related features.

Exploratory question

Proposes what to examine next.

≠

Diagnostic judgment

Externally observable material supports a conclusion with bounded confidence.

Strong judgment established

Proportionate object, evidence, scale, responsibility, and observation gates are satisfied.

≠

Action may be taken

Still requires normative, authorization, procedural, and protective conditions.

Strength of concept use

This section limits what the current statement can bear.

≠

S states or personality rankings

The five levels cannot replace another classification or assess human worth.

Teaching construction: matching clothing and a shared taskTeaching scenario

AssumptionsBoth groups are teaching hypotheses, not actual field studies.

A calls everyone wearing blue in a square a collaborative structure, but lacks material on interaction, shared problems, or maintenance costs; at most, the set can first be described. B observes repair workers across cities repeatedly sharing parts, taking up work orders, and bearing waiting costs, with error feedback changing subsequent allocations. This provides material for further checks of formal mapping. B still gains no qualification to diagnose every member's motives or discipline members.

BoundaryActual boundaries and repeated influence require material; one fragment of task collaboration cannot directly certify them either.

Teaching construction: bad news cannot reach actionTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe process and events are constructed; no organization was investigated.

A hypothetical process has a complaints mailbox, but all messages are automatically archived and decision-makers lack the authority or channel to adjust accordingly. The mailbox's existence supports only a description of an entry point, not the claim that bad news can change subsequent practice. If review is later enabled and an error actually corrected, the material supports only that particular change. General effectiveness needs later observation.

BoundaryAbsence of a particular change does not alone establish an absence of correction capacity; a correct original decision can be retained after reasoned review.

Teaching construction: diagnosis cannot jump into disciplineTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA hypothetical scheduling situation illustrating argumentative layers only; no actual employment action is recommended.

Suppose external observations give a researcher low-to-moderate-confidence grounds to suspect that a scheduling relationship creates persistent burdens. The diagnosis and unknowns can be stated; a supervisor cannot immediately revoke people's eligibility based on this conceptual label. Stronger assertions need further evidence, and action still requires a justified target, permissions, procedures, and protections.

BoundaryThis example does not determine specific institutions' legal or permission conditions, nor has diagnostic accuracy been verified.

Actual classification text: scope and conditions in the IAU planet definitionDocumented case

IAU Resolution B5 of 2006 specifies the Solar System as its scope and lists conditions including orbiting the Sun, being nearly round, and clearing the orbital neighborhood. B6 classifies Pluto as a dwarf planet under that definition. What is directly observable here is a professional institution organizing names through explicit scope and conditions, rather than using an old name to prove its own classification.

16.6GOV-06 Absence Signals, Protective Opacity, and Suppressive Opacity ​

In briefNo complaints in a place may mean the relevant problem is genuinely absent, or that people fear speaking, lack somewhere to speak, or cannot leave a lasting record. Judging whether hidden information is justified requires more than “how much was disclosed”: ask whom it protects, who benefits, who can review it, and when the protective rationale is reconsidered.

What is not visible can still carry information. Absence of an anchor may mean no shared orientation ever formed. Absence of feedback may mean there is no channel or people are afraid to speak. Absence of conflict may come from fear, dependence, or punishment. Absence of repair may mean there is no interface for it. Absence of exit may mean the cost of leaving is unbearable. Absence of language may mean people lack the means to express themselves.

Opacity has three kinds.

protected. Protects vulnerable subjects, privacy, witness safety, experience that is still taking shape, and feedback from people with little power.

functional. Reduces information overload and preserves room for necessary professional judgment, ritual, buffering, or undisturbed decision-making. It requires subsequent review and tracing of responsibility.

suppressive. Obscures responsibility, blocks feedback, evades review, produces fear, preserves a monopoly on power, or prevents people who were harmed from proving the harm.

Classification must answer four questions. Who is protected? Who benefits? Who can review independently? When is the opacity lifted? Opacity must not be recorded as a healthy boundary if the four answers, independent review, time limits, or conditions for lifting it are incomplete. Suppressive opacity directly triggers measures against capture, external review, and a block on public release.

The time limits and conditions for lifting opacity govern continued review of the grounds for confidentiality. They do not require sensitive material to be disclosed automatically on a particular date. Review may continue protection or disclose only what is sufficient for a limited judgment. Inability to confirm that opacity is justified does not establish suppression. A confidentiality label also cannot conceal falsified records, evasion of responsibility, or obstruction of credible verification.

16.6Note

Understanding this section

16.6 GOV-06 Absence Signals, Protective Opacity, and Suppressive Opacity

No complaints in a place may mean the relevant problem is genuinely absent, or that people fear speaking, lack somewhere to speak, or cannot leave a lasting record. Judging whether hidden information is justified requires more than “how much was disclosed”: ask whom it protects, who benefits, who can review it, and when the protective rationale is reconsidered.

The signals of absence listed in this section are possible explanations to distinguish, not a diagnosis of suppression whenever silence appears. An absent anchor may mean a shared orientation never formed; absent feedback may mean no channel exists or people fear speaking; absent conflict may reflect fear, dependence, or punishment; absent repair may mean there is no interface; absent exit may mean the price of leaving is unbearable; absent language may mean a lack of expressive tools. They shift inquiry from “whether a surface record exists” to the conditions of formation, expression, transmission, and detection. One explanation cannot cover every setting.

For example, “nobody exits” is compatible with at least two situations: people want to stay, or they find leaving difficult. Distinguishing them calls for checking alternatives, exit costs, punishment risks, anonymous views, and subsequent responses, rather than forcing people to state their positions publicly on the spot. Likewise, lacking formal language does not mean lacking experience, and lacking conflict records does not mean agreement. Absence has research value, but its interpretation depends on observation conditions. This connects both to 16.4's prohibition on filling missing evidence with zeros and to Part Seven's point that observational intervention can change the object.

protected concerns protecting vulnerable actors, privacy, witness safety, experience not yet fully formed, and low-power feedback. Concealing reporters' identities can coexist with preserving verifiable content; privacy does not exempt powerful people from responsibility. Protection should consider indirect identification: even after names are removed, combinations of rare roles, dates, and places may expose individuals. This states the need for proportionate protection, not a promise that any anonymization method is absolutely safe, nor a requirement that people first expose themselves to prove harm.

functional is the bounded opacity needed to reduce information overload, preserve professional judgment, ritual space, buffer zones, or quiet space for decisions, while permitting subsequent review and tracing of responsibility. Temporarily withholding discussion from public view can prevent unprocessed speculation from immediately harming others; it cannot justify making decision grounds permanently uncheckable or responsible persons forever unanswerable. Professional expertise is no substitute for independent review either; specify who can see what under which authorization and protection.

suppressive is characterized by concealing responsibility, blocking feedback, evading review, creating fear, maintaining monopolies of power, or preventing harmed people from proving harm. Judgment requires material about relevant conduct and consequences, rather than only managers' accounts of their motives. A real arrangement may reasonably keep some content confidential while blocking verification of other content. Examine these separately by object and use instead of applying a permanent label to an entire organization. Once proportionate material establishes suppressive opacity, the source requires triggering anti-capture measures, external review, and a block on public release; it must not continue to be treated as a healthy boundary.

All three classifications must answer four questions: whom does it protect, who benefits, who can independently review it, and when is it lifted? Without complete answers, independent review, time boundaries, and lifting conditions, it must not be registered as a healthy boundary. This does not require publishing the real names of protected people on a public page. Appropriate role descriptions and controlled verification can identify protected positions, authorization, and the responsibility chain while maintaining safety. Blocking public release also does not mean publishing sensitive material to punish failures of duty. Restrict eligibility for the relevant public judgments that depend on this opacity, and follow proportionate review and protection procedures.

Durations and lifting conditions manage continuing review of confidentiality grounds; they are not countdowns to exposing private information. An expiry review may conclude that protection remains necessary or that only the portion needed to support a bounded judgment should be disclosed. Preserve responsibility records of who maintained, adjusted, or lifted protection on what grounds. Failure to confirm justification does not establish suppression; conversely, a confidentiality label cannot shield fabrication, evasion of responsibility, or obstruction of credible verification. There is an important third state: justification remains unconfirmed, so suspend healthy-boundary certification while continuing inquiry.

The strongest objection is that greater requirements for records and review can expose the very people meant to be protected. This risk is real, so access to material and public disclosure must be minimized, and reviewers must also be constrained by corresponding protection and authority. The solution is neither to abolish review nor to disclose everything to everyone. Distinguish sensitive content, evidence needed to support bounded conclusions, independent verifiers, and explanations visible to the public. Assessment should also consider the exposure and burdens that further questions impose on participants; when information is insufficient, narrow the conclusion rather than compel disclosure.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Separate visible records from actual states and list multiple distinguishable explanations of absence.

  2. 2

    Check conditions of expression channels, prices to be paid, detection, and observational intervention; silence does not directly establish health or suppression.

  3. 3

    Assess the object and use of protected, functional, or suppressive classifications item by item, checking the four questions and independent review.

  4. 4

    When conditions are incomplete, first refuse healthy-boundary certification; when suppression is actually evidenced, trigger the corresponding anti-capture measures, review, and release block.

  5. 5

    Review timing and lifting conditions do not mean automatic disclosure; maintaining protection also requires proportionate reasons and a responsibility trail.

Distinctions to keep clear

No conflict records are visible

Describes the state of available material.

≠

No conflict exists, or suppression is established

Both are judgments about the object requiring additional material.

Protective opacity

Limits exposure to protect vulnerable positions and safe feedback.

≠

Suppressive opacity

Blocks verification, feedback, or pursuit of responsibility, among other things.

Functional opacity

Has necessary reasons and permits subsequent review and accountability.

≠

Professionals cannot be questioned

Exempts verification through status and fails the required conditions.

Review due

Check whether protective reasons still hold and how to adjust them.

≠

Sensitive information automatically becomes public at expiry

The source explicitly does not require this.

Teaching construction: two sources of zero complaintsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe two teams and their membership counts are hypothetical; no real personnel survey was conducted.

All ten members of team A can safely raise objections at low cost, yet no complaints arise; team B also has zero complaints, but its manager punishes reporters. The figure “0” alone cannot distinguish them. Check channels, risks, retention of material, and safe feedback. If that information is also unavailable, the conclusion should be that zero records cannot certify health, not that suppression of team B's kind has directly been established.

BoundaryEven observing an available channel cannot guarantee every problem will be reported; no statistical detection model has been established.

Teaching construction: maintaining protection when review is dueTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe duration and report are design examples, not a real case or regulatory requirement.

Suppose the confidentiality grounds for a witness report are reviewed every three months. At review time, credible material indicates that identity-exposure risk persists. Independent review can maintain protection while publishing de-identified conclusions and bounded supporting grounds. Reaching the date does not authorize publishing the name; responsibility for the next review and conditions for lifting protection remain.

BoundaryThree months is not a universal duration; specific arrangements depend on risks, authorization, and applicable procedures.

Teaching construction: different responsibilities within one documentTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe meeting is constructed; no actual identity or document is disclosed.

Imagined meeting minutes contain statements identifying harmed people and the grounds for managerial decisions. Public disclosure of the former may be restricted; if even authorized independent review of the latter is blocked, merely saying “protecting privacy” is insufficient. Material and access permissions can be separated to support responsibility tracing with less exposure; unverified facts still cannot be treated as confirmed accusations.

BoundarySeparation may not achieve complete anonymity; if re-identification remains possible, publicly disclosable content should be narrowed further.

An actual mechanism: NASA ASRS de-identified reportsDocumented case

The official NASA ASRS website explains that reports are voluntary, personal and organizational names are removed before database entry, and dates, times, and other potentially identifying details are generalized or removed. This example shows that preserving safety information and reducing identity exposure can be designed separately. The website also lists confidentiality exceptions, so the mechanism description cannot be understood as a guarantee of absolute confidentiality for all material.

SourceOfficial NASA ASRS website, checked on 2026-10-14Paragraphs 1–2 of Confidentiality and Incentives to Report; for exceptions, see the first separately listed CaveatReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsOnly the official mechanism description was checked. This does not independently certify successful protection of every report or improved accident rates, nor discuss individual waiver eligibility. The two pages do not suffice to certify all four GOV-06 questions.

What does not follow

16.7GOV-07 Operating Limits of Stage 6 and Stopping Observational Recursion ​

In briefBeing able to repair a fault does not mean the whole organization has reached some highest stage. To assess S6 here, first check whether the object is an applicable human collective, which functions and periods the evidence covers, and when further questioning must stop.
Codes used in this section (1)
  • S6Prototype of Adaptive Dynamic Balance

The qualified reference for this module is governance.module.GOV-07 → hsp.domain.human_intentional_collective → hsp.state.S6. It applies only to objects that independent runtime records confirm are human intentional collectives and whose status includes hsp.state.S6. It does not apply to individual humans, nonhuman systems, or human collectives that have yet to meet S6. Stage 6 here is no universal level of the world broadly conceived.

Stage 6 does not transcend entropy increase or describe a perfect system. For a specified function, object, and limited window, it requires evidence of problem detection, correction of errors, restoration of function, and continuity when others take over. It must also meet the conditions of applicability in Part 8. Record detection lag, repair lag, recurrence rates, resource margins, and load distribution separately. Processes measured in different units must not be combined into a single speed. Current operation that is going well can support a judgment about the corresponding function. It cannot by itself certify Stage 6. Genuine recovery under continuing support does not automatically cease to count because support has yet to be removed.

Observational recursion may expand only when a new response changes boundaries, identity, resources, channels for action, uptake relationships, feedback write-back, risk, or public memory, or supplies a new signal that is costly to produce. Recursion must end when two consecutive rounds yield only the same kind of response, the object begins manipulating diagnostic rules, continued tracking would increase exposure, the informational gain is less than the disruption to the structure, or the diagnostician can no longer distinguish the object’s state from the products of observation.

After stopping, do not keep asking “what the object really is.” State only that a particular response pattern can be confirmed under current observation conditions. Further judgment requires external review or new external evidence that distinguishes the alternatives.

16.7Note

Understanding this section

16.7 GOV-07 Operational Boundaries of Stage 6 and Closure of Observational Recursion

Being able to repair a fault does not mean the whole organization has reached some highest stage. To assess S6 here, first check whether the object is an applicable human collective, which functions and periods the evidence covers, and when further questioning must stop.

This module's bounded reference is governance.module.GOV-07 → hsp.domain.human_intentional_collective → hsp.state.S6. The arrows indicate references to the domain of application and state, not a causal chain or evolutionary ladder. An independent runtime record must establish that the object is a human intentional collective and that its state includes S6. Individual humans, nonhuman systems, and collectives not meeting S6 cannot be directly included. A record number or internal assertion cannot replace Part Eight's required object evidence, identity, scale, window, independent review, and counterevidence checks.

“A state includes” does not require masking differences with a single label for the whole. Part Eight permits evidence-based distinctions among single_dominant, mixed, parallel, and unknown; the two multi-prototype configurations, mixed and parallel, require positive material, and the unknown cannot masquerade as a mixture. If one subsystem meets S6 while other positions do not, preserve the corresponding scope rather than extrapolating local recovery to the entire institution. All states remain descriptive judgments: they generate no action authorization and do not imply greater worth than other people or collectives.

S6 requires corresponding evidence of problem detection, error correction, functional recovery, and continuity of those taking up the work within specified functions, objects, and bounded windows. §8.3.7 additionally requires distributed uptake, effective feedback, recovery and renewal, and new generative capabilities: multiple positions can correct errors with little central intervention, and successors genuinely gain knowledge, authority, and protection and can change old arrangements. Low fluctuation, constant firefighting by a central figure, frequent personnel turnover, and polished annual reports can produce similar appearances and cannot alone certify S6.

Stage 6 is not transcendence of entropy increase, absence of conflict, or permanent immunity to failure. The source's dynamic equilibrium means bounded maintenance of functions through continuing calibration; regression, splitting, transition, exit, or collapse remain possible. Good current operation supports the corresponding functional judgment but may not test recovery from disturbances or continuity of uptake. Conversely, genuine recovery is not automatically invalid because it needs continuing support. Distinguish autonomous, transferable resource backing from irreplaceable, hidden, single-point firefighting. Safety support must not be withdrawn without authorization merely to demonstrate adaptation.

Record detection delays, repair delays, recurrence rates, resource margins, and load distribution separately. Delays have starting and ending times and time units; recurrence rates have events and opportunity denominators; margins specify resource types; load also concerns who bears it. Do not add hours, proportions, inventories, and headcounts into one “unified speed,” or use averages to conceal prolonged overload at peripheral positions. Causal effects also require proportionate identification; observing recovery during support does not automatically establish that any one measure caused it.

Observational recursion means the object responds to diagnosis, and the response enters the next observation round. Further expansion has an entry point only when a new response changes boundaries, identity, resources, action channels, uptake relations, feedback write-back, risks, or public memory, or provides a new high-cost signal. More similar statements, changed wording, or additional documents from the same source do not automatically count as new discriminating evidence. Even when an entry point appears, safety and stopping conditions still constrain further tracking.

Five situations require closure: two consecutive rounds yield only responses of the same kind; the object starts manipulating diagnostic rules; tracking increases exposure; information gains fall below structural disturbance; or the diagnostician can no longer distinguish object states from products of observation. These are procedural stopping conditions, not proof that the object is permanently unintelligible, nor that anyone adjusting behavior when questioned intends deception. Manipulation of diagnostic rules requires specific material; refusal of unsafe disclosure cannot be treated as malice. Two rounds of same-kind responses is this section's explicit rule, not an empirically calibrated optimal number of rounds for every study.

After closure, do not keep asking what the object ‘really is.’ Instead, give a conditional result: a certain response pattern can be confirmed under the current observational conditions; stronger judgments require external review or new external evidence with discriminatory power. Retain established local facts, while limiting the relevant classification where crucial material is insufficient. The strongest objection is that stopping could allow hidden problems to persist. The response is to retain the risks, evidence, and access to safe external review, rather than create new exposure through endless repeated questioning and then treat the resulting reactions as the object's essence.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Check the applicable domain of GOV-07 using independent runtime evidence of the object and its state; stop applying it if the requirements are unmet.

  2. 2

    Freeze the function, scale, window, and identity, and examine discovery, correction, recovery, and continuity of uptake separately.

  3. 3

    Check similar appearances and counterevidence, distinguishing continuing support, dependence on a single point, and current effective operation.

  4. 4

    Record lags, recurrence, margins, and loads separately in their respective units; causal claims and extrapolation require additional, proportionate evidence.

  5. 5

    Expand only when new responses exhibit the specified structural changes. Stop recursion when any closure condition is triggered, and report a conditional pattern and the evidence needed next.

Distinctions to keep clear

Genuine functional recovery

A bounded function recovers under specified conditions.

≠

Certification of S6 as a whole

This still requires evidence of the applicable domain, the complete prototype, uptake, and other conditions.

Continuing support

Resource backstops can coexist with genuine autonomy and continuity.

≠

Irreplaceable firefighting at a single point

This may allow apparent stability to conceal fragility.

New material obtained through observation

This can distinguish changes in boundaries, channels, risks, and other features.

≠

Repeated responses of the same kind

These cannot indefinitely justify further questioning.

Closure

Limit what can be judged under the current observation and seek external evidence.

≠

A permanent conclusion about essence

Stopping recursion does not prove that the object will always be this way or cannot be understood.

Mathematical construction: even identical time units require an explicit chain of eventsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe time points, counts, and set of opportunities are all stipulated, not observed repair data.

Suppose a fault occurs at t=0 hours, is discovered at t=2, and the specified repair is completed at t=7. If discovery lag is defined as the interval from occurrence to discovery, and repair lag as the interval from discovery to completion, these are 2 hours and 5 hours respectively, with 7 hours elapsed overall. If recurrence separately occurs in 2 of 20 appropriate observation opportunities, the recurrence proportion is 2/20=10%. The 7 hours and 10% cannot be added to obtain a ‘repair speed.’ The first two durations can be combined into total elapsed time only if their start and end points are explicit and the intervals are contiguous.

BoundaryCompleting a repair does not automatically establish subsequent functioning or long-term absence of recurrence; the actual denominator and observation window require separate verification.

Teaching construction: recovery without withdrawing supportTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe teams, recovery, and permissions are conditional assumptions; no organizational experiment was conducted.

A hypothetical collaborative team restores a service while backup resources continue to be supplied, and its successors have acquired the knowledge and authority to stop. The fact that support has not been withdrawn does not erase the recovery. Whether S6 is reached still requires checking autonomy across multiple positions, actual handover, and counterevidence. Another team's stability depends entirely on one leader secretly firefighting. An identical appearance does not justify the same prototype judgment.

BoundaryThis example does not recommend withdrawing resources as a challenge experiment; verification must proceed under safe authorization.

Teaching construction: when to stop questioningTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe interviews and responses are a teaching construction, not actual research records.

Suppose a hypothetical investigation receives only defensive answers of the same kind in two consecutive rounds, with no new material about boundaries or channels; further questioning could expose members with little power. The conclusion should be limited to ‘this kind of response occurs under the current interview conditions.’ Retain the known risks and seek safe, independent material. Do not keep pressing until a story matching the diagnostician's expectations emerges.

BoundaryDefensive answers do not by themselves prove deception, repression, or failure to reach S6; external material is needed to distinguish these possibilities.

Real technical recovery: the limits of judgment concerning the 2009 Hubble servicing missionDocumented case

NASA Goddard's archive records that the SM4 mission serviced Hubble on May 11–24, 2009, repaired the previously failed STIS and ACS instruments, and installed equipment including batteries and gyroscopes. This official historical account supports discussion of specific repairs. It does not support classifying the telescope itself as a human collective at S6, or certifying uptake and governance throughout NASA solely on the basis of the mission's success.

SourceNASA GSFC, archived introduction to SM4Paragraphs 1–3 of the Introduction; the top of the page explicitly identifies it as an archive that is no longer updatedReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsUsed only to verify historical repair facts. Complete performance and organizational runtime records were not obtained, and the page's old predictions about future years are not treated as current facts.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe device can recover automatically, so it has entered S6.

What it limitsA device falls outside the applicable domain of human intentional collectives. Its recovery can be established for a domain-specific task without receiving an S6 classification.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleResource support has not been withdrawn, so all recovery is fake.

What it limitsContinuing support does not automatically negate genuine recovery; autonomy, continuity, and dependence on a single point must be checked.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleThe more questions we ask, the better we understand the essence; refusal to answer also proves the diagnosis correct.

What it limitsRecursion can create exposure and observational artifacts. Judgment must be limited once closure conditions are met.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • S6 applies only to qualifying human intentional collectives, not to individual personalities, devices, or the universe.
  • Keep local and overall judgments, and current functioning and continuity of uptake, separate; unknown is not mixed.
  • Do not remove necessary support or create disturbances without authorization to test recovery capacity.
  • The two-round rule is a governance condition stipulated by the text, not a natural law or a universally optimal sample size.
  • A history of technical repair does not establish an S6 runtime classification for the organization concerned.

Scope and open questions

The actual repair serves as a boundary case showing that functional recovery and S6 classification are not interchangeable; it does not invent S6 certification for a real organization.

  • No S6 runtime classification has been established for any real human collective, and no recursive observation has been conducted.
  • NASA's historical summary does not provide all the evidence of discovery lags, recurrence rates, load distributions, and uptake required in this section.

16.8GOV-08 Malicious Compliance and Auditing Selective Evidence ​

In briefForms, evidence chains, and appeals can all appear complete while only favorable material is allowed into the conclusion. This section examines whether these procedures are used selectively, rather than whether they have names. The risk rules first limit strong judgments; they do not convict people by counting checked boxes.

Malicious compliance occurs when forms, evidence chains, reviews, and appeals are completed selectively while sources are still manipulated, weak signals filtered, inaction dressed up, or responsibility obscured. It differs from open violation. Check each of ten signals. There is only one source. Counterexamples are dismissed as noise or emotion. Open assertions become labels. Appeals never change outcomes. Supposedly independent parties are controlled by the same chain of power. AI reports lack original materials and external verification. Diagnostic language is used to justify inaction or avoid accountability. Potential fields, entropy increase, and stages are used to dress up inaction. Love, mission, the larger interest, or professional expertise are invoked to continue extracting from people with little power. People who appeal are subsequently described as irrational because they appealed.

Three or more signals block strong judgments. At five or more signals, record a high risk of malicious compliance. Only risk registration, a request for external review, and exploratory steps for protection may then be output. The party audited cannot certify the reviewer’s independence.

Three and five are procedural thresholds for starting protection and review. They are neither constants read from nature nor calibrated probabilities of malice. A trigger means a strong judgment should not proceed under present conditions. It does not establish that anyone deliberately deceived others. Review must state dependencies among the signals, costs of false alarms and misses, and the particular circumstances. Any change to the thresholds should disclose its grounds through the version procedure. Thresholds must not be changed on the spot after a case outcome is known.

16.8Note

Understanding this section

16.8 GOV-08 Malicious compliance and selective evidence auditing

Forms, evidence chains, and appeals can all appear complete while only favorable material is allowed into the conclusion. This section examines whether these procedures are used selectively, rather than whether they have names. The risk rules first limit strong judgments; they do not convict people by counting checked boxes.

Malicious compliance means selectively completing forms, evidence chains, reviews, and appeals while manipulating sources, filtering weak signals, dressing up inaction, or laundering responsibility. It differs from openly refusing rules and must not be confused with ordinary incomplete material, inexperience, or reasonable protective confidentiality. Auditing requires material about actual sources, permissions, actions, and consequences. ‘Many formalities’ alone prove neither honesty nor malicious intent.

The ten signals must be checked individually. First, a single source: do apparently numerous documents all trace back to one supplier, without proportionate external material? Second, counterexamples downgraded to noise or emotion: are there verifiable reasons for excluding them, or are they deleted simply because they are unfavorable? Third, open assertions turned into labels: statements that were conditional and revisable become fixed judgments of a person's or object's nature. Fourth, appeals never change outcomes: investigate whether reasoned corrections of errors are institutionally blocked, rather than demanding a reversal on every appeal. Reasoned confirmation of a correct original decision can still make the appeal effective.

Fifth, independent parties controlled by the same chain of power: different identities do not ensure independence if funding, evaluation, promotion, or control relationships make independence difficult. Sixth, AI reports without original material and external verification: polished language and numerous citations do not fulfill evidentiary responsibilities; the availability of source documents and their consistency with claims still require checking. Seventh, diagnostic language used to justify inaction or avoidance of accountability: analysis becomes an excuse to delay authorized, necessary, feasible action on responsibility, rather than proportionate risk control. Conversely, not every reasoned suspension of high-risk action should be treated as malicious.

Eighth, potential fields, entropy increase, or stages used to dress up inaction: abstract inevitability erases responsibility conditions that could have been changed, without examining specific channels and constraints. Ninth, love, mission, the greater good, or expertise used to continue extracting from low-power actors: examine loads, exit, compensation, feedback, and permissions, rather than convicting on the basis of attractive words alone. Tenth, appellants relabeled as irrational because they appeal: the act of objecting is circularly treated as grounds to deny their credibility, creating a label that prevents correction. Whether their actual statements are inaccurate can still be examined, but ‘you object, so you are the problem’ cannot close off appeals.

At three or more signals, block strong judgments. At five or more, register a high risk of malicious compliance and output only risk registration, requests for external review, and protective probes. The second threshold incorporates the first threshold's restrictions; reaching five does not restore permission for strong assertions. Fewer than three signals is not a certificate of health either: one serious instance of fabricated evidence or missing permission may already suffice under another contract to block the corresponding output. Protective probes here must remain within authorized, safe, low-exposure boundaries; auditing cannot be used as a pretext for punishment, deception, or intrusion.

Three and five are procedural thresholds chosen by the text, not natural constants, and no calibration is supplied that converts counts into probabilities of malicious intent. Five signals does not mean 50% maliciousness, nor eight signals 80%. Signals may also depend on a common source: one chain of power controlling material and review can simultaneously produce a single source, nonindependent reviewers, and ineffective appeals. Registration must explain the factual grounds for each item and the relationships among them. It must neither count one repeated sentence as several signals nor assume that the ten signals are independent trials and multiply probabilities.

Triggering a threshold means only that continuing strong judgments is currently inappropriate and that protective review is needed; it does not establish that someone deliberately deceived others. Review must also consider the costs and contexts of false positives and false negatives. False positives may harm those audited and legitimate confidentiality; false negatives may allow disadvantaged people to remain exposed to harm. If thresholds need adjustment, the grounds should be explained through a public versioning procedure, rather than changing the number after seeing a case's outcome so that it just avoids triggering. External authorization and appeal protections cannot be arbitrarily canceled by a threshold.

An audited party cannot certify its own reviewer's independence. Auditors may use identity and relationship information supplied by that party, but judgments of independence also require verifiable material and an appropriate independent procedure. The strongest objection is that these signals are so broad that they treat all caution and professional confidentiality as malicious. The response is to record evidence for each signal, retain competing explanations, distinguish risk from intent, and narrow outputs according to dependencies, rather than label people by an overall impression. A genuine audit must allow its own signal judgments to be found mistaken and corrected, instead of becoming another tool of malicious compliance.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Examine the ten signals and original material individually; do not substitute the number of formalities or writing style for actual effects and relationships.

  2. 2

    Record the facts, alternative explanations, and signal dependencies for each item; do not force unknowns into boxes marked as having occurred.

  3. 3

    At 3 signals, block strong judgments; at 5, enter the stricter scope of risk outputs. Even below a threshold, check other stopping conditions.

  4. 4

    Preserve the distinction between procedural risk and a finding of deliberate deception, and use independent review and safe protections.

  5. 5

    If changing a threshold, explain the grounds through the versioning procedure and retain the original rule and the case's history.

Distinctions to keep clear

Formal completion

Documents such as forms, reviews, and appeals exist.

≠

Substantive corrigibility

Unfavorable facts can enter the process, reasoned errors can be corrected, and consequences can be borne.

A procedural threshold is triggered

Initiate protection, restrict outputs, and conduct review.

≠

Probability of malicious intent or a finding of guilt

These require different evidence and procedures; counts cannot establish them automatically.

Multiple signals are present

Different checklist items may simultaneously have factual support.

≠

Statistical independence

A list alone does not justify assuming independence or multiplying probabilities.

A decision upheld on reasoned appeal

After checking the material, a correct decision is maintained on sufficient grounds.

≠

Appeals structurally blocked

Even valid evidence of error cannot change the outcome.

Formal construction: a threshold boundary is not a probabilityTeaching scenario

Assumptionsn is an integer input for teaching, not an actual audit result, and no probability model has been fitted.

Define n as the number of distinct signals among the ten supported by proportionate material. Under this counting rule, n=2 does not trigger the three-signal check; n=3 and 4 block strong judgments; n=5 through 10 restrict outputs to the high-risk scope while continuing to block strong judgments. n=0 through 2 does not qualify a case for strong judgment, because object, evidence, authorization, and other checks must still be met. If 3 signals are correlated, the count can still trigger the rule, but one cannot claim that three independent pieces of evidence multiply the probability of malicious intent to a particular value.

BoundaryUnknown signals and dependencies must be recorded separately; three copies concerning the same checklist item cannot be counted as three signals.

Teaching construction: many documents, one sourceTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe report and number of links are constructed; no real AI product was audited.

An imagined AI report lists 20 links, but tracing them shows they all reproduce the same organization’s press release, with no original observations. Their common source and the gap in verification of original material can be recorded. The 20 links cannot alone count as independent evidence, nor do they automatically establish malicious intent by the writer. If the report’s task was only to study how that organization describes itself, these texts may still be useful within that limited task.

BoundaryThe risk significance of a single source depends on the specific task. Material from a common source may serve as discourse evidence, but cannot pose as external verification of facts.

Teaching construction: justified suspension and laundering of responsibilityTeaching scenario

AssumptionsBoth management situations are teaching assumptions, not decisions concerning real organizations or legal advice.

An imagined manager suspends punishment because evidence is insufficient and the action irreversible, and starts a time-limited independent inquiry: this is a defensible stop. Another arrangement repeatedly says, “The system is in a certain stage, so investigation is unnecessary,” and refuses an authorized inquiry into responsibility. That supplies a clue of inaction requiring further audit. Neither has imposed punishment yet, but their reasons, procedures, and consequences differ.

BoundaryWithout material, wording alone cannot establish motives; risk registration does not authorize punishment either.

An actual regulatory record: the appearance of compliance under test conditionsDocumented case

On September 18, 2015, the EPA issued a press release about its notice of violation concerning Volkswagen. It described software in certain vehicles that detected official emissions tests and fully activated emissions controls only during testing; it also explained that the agencies pursued their investigation after outside research raised questions. This record illustrates how ‘performance within the test’ can diverge from normal operation and the role of external material.

SourceUS EPA, press release of 2015-09-18Press release of 2015-09-18: opening paragraph; paragraph beginning As described in the NOV; paragraph beginning EPA and CARB uncoveredReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis records the investigation and allegations announced by the EPA at that time. It does not rescore Volkswagen using the ten signals, or infer individual subjective motives, all vehicle models, final adjudications, or current legal effects from that page.

What does not follow

  • Fewer than 3 signals does not confer a safety certificate; other evidence, permission, and protection checks can still independently block an output.
  • Neither 3 nor 5 signals is a natural constant or a calibrated risk probability.
  • Do not count unknowns as either no problem or a triggered signal; insufficient evidence can separately limit the corresponding strong judgment.

Scope and open questions

The actual regulator’s original release shows that procedural measurements can be selectively accommodated. It supports only a narrow analogy, not a field audit using this framework.

  • No real object has undergone a complete item-by-item audit of the ten checks, nor has threshold effectiveness been calibrated.
  • The costs of false alarms and missed detections require context-specific material; this lesson does not invent test results.

How do the procedural outputs differ at 4 and 5 signals?

Four items already block strong judgments. Five additionally require registration of high risk and limit outputs to risk registration, requests for external review, and protective probes; they do not restore strong judgments.

16.9GOV-09 AI Boundaries and What Process Outputs Can Establish ​

In briefAn AI report may offer excellent arguments and help choose an option. But writing “verification completed” cannot make a nonexistent source real or turn unimplemented protection and repair into reality. The question is what actually grounds each conclusion.

AI can organize materials and verify their identity, propose and compare mechanisms, form grounded judgments and critiques that can be refuted, recommend options under disclosed objectives, normative premises, and constraints, and draft institutional arrangements, plans, and commentary for deliberation. Outputs should state the current choice, key grounds, costs, strongest opposing case, and conditions that would change it. They should also present in full the substantive analysis already conducted. AI must not invent sources or protection conditions. Fluent text, internal scores, and completion of a procedure cannot establish the commissioning party’s good faith, effective anti-retaliation, or actual repair. AI cannot substitute for independent review or bearing responsibility. It cannot independently make a high-risk real-world decision or substitute a claim that the procedure passed for a decision by a subject with authority. An analytical recommendation does not amount to actual adoption. High-risk decisions and real-world execution still require the applicable procedures for strong judgments, protection, normative choice, and authorization.

AI outputs should check original facts, testimony from affected positions, counterexamples, feedback from people with little power, external review, records of appeals changing outcomes, who controls the evidence, and AI’s selection and rewriting of material, according to the task and proposed conclusion. For each, state how it relates to the conclusion, whether it is available, and what limits follow from its absence. The count of missing items alone does not determine the ceiling for the whole output. Do not make a factual finding without decisive evidence for it. Retain competing explanations when causal identification lacks discriminating evidence. Without adequate protection and review, do not certify actual safety, consent, fairness, repair, or eligibility for high-impact adoption. Evaluations of arguments in texts, local factual judgments, and conditional recommendations under explicit premises that are unaffected by the gaps can stand separately. Give reasons for any finding of inapplicability. It must not substitute for an unknown or bypass a real risk. Outputs still governed by strong-judgment and real-world action provisions remain subject to their requirements.

Process outputs do not establish what holds in reality. Fluent prose, automatic scoring, internal stress tests, consistency matrices, validation passes, report counts, and complete forms cannot establish repair, consent, safety, or effectiveness.

16.9Note

Understanding this section

16.9 GOV-09 AI Boundaries and the Non-Proof Status of Process Products

An AI report may offer excellent arguments and help choose an option. But writing “verification completed” cannot make a nonexistent source real or turn unimplemented protection and repair into reality. The question is what actually grounds each conclusion.

This section allows AI to do substantive work: organize material and verify its identity; propose and compare mechanisms; formulate grounded, refutable judgments and criticism; recommend options under public goals and normative constraints; and draft institutions, plans, and commentary for deliberation. It does not require AI always to summarize or abstain. Analysis performed should be presented as a full, inspectable substantive argument: what is currently chosen, why, its costs, the strongest opposing case, and what conditions would change the choice. What is required here is verifiable reasoning and analytical results, not self-scoring or empty announcements of process in place of content.

AI must not fabricate sources or protective conditions. Even complete source titles, URLs, and citation formats require checking the object’s identity, version, and actual scope of support. “There is an appeal procedure” requires examination of accessibility and substantive review and correction capacity. Fluent prose cannot prove a commissioning party’s integrity, effective protection against retaliation, or real repair; internal scores and process completion cannot replace independent review and responsibility. AI can distinguish a source’s existence from its support for different propositions, but cannot end this verification by issuing its own certificate.

An analytical recommendation is not actual adoption, and drafting an institution does not mean an authorized actor has approved it or it has taken effect. High-risk real-world decisions and execution still require procedures for strong judgments, protection, normative choice, and authorization. AI cannot make such decisions independently or pass off “the process passed” as a decision by an authorized actor. Even when recommendation conditions hold, who may decide, how appeals work, and what is revocable require separate checks. When people’s rights or opportunities are affected, automatically generated conclusions must especially not be converted directly into action against them.

Task-evidence checks cover eight groups of material: original facts, testimony from affected positions, counterexamples, low-power feedback, external review, records of appeals changing outcomes, relationships of control over evidence, and AI’s own selection and rewriting of material. Original-fact checks trace initial objects and versions; testimony and low-power feedback supply positions invisible in central narratives; counterexamples test whether only positives were selected; external review checks actual independence; appeal records check whether errors can be changed; control relationships check who can delete, alter, or obstruct evidence; and AI selection and rewriting checks for omitted qualifications, correlation rewritten as causation, or unknown rewritten as negative.

Not every item applies equally to every task. For each, explain its relationship to the current conclusion, whether it is available, and what its absence limits. “Not applicable” needs a reason. For example, checking only whether a formal derivation is valid under explicit assumptions may not require real appeal cases; claiming that an institution is fair or feedback is safe may make those materials critical. Difficulty obtaining material does not make it inapplicable, and vulnerable people must not be forced into exposure to fill evidence gaps. Keep unknown, unobservable, and not applicable separate, narrowing the conclusion where necessary.

Missing material limits conclusions according to dependencies, rather than uniformly downgrading every output based on the number of missing fields. Missing key factual evidence prevents that factual finding; missing evidence distinguishing causes leaves competing explanations open; insufficient protection and review prevent certification of actual safety, consent, fairness, repair, or eligibility for high-impact adoption. Unaffected assessments of textual arguments, local factual judgments, and conditional recommendations under explicit premises may still hold separately. If a shared critical premise fails, several dependent conclusions may lose their grounds together, but explain the shared dependence rather than rejecting or approving everything on an overall impression.

Process products include fluent text, automated scores, internal stress tests, consistency matrices, validator passes, report counts, and complete tables. They may establish limited process facts, such as JSON satisfying structural constraints or a set of artificial tests returning no errors, but not real-world repair, consent, safety, or effectiveness. A validator can check only the rules and inputs supplied to it; passing is unsurprising when the rules omit actual risks. Conversely, a process defect does not automatically negate a fact supported by independent material.

The strongest objection is that these requirements would leave AI unable ever to advise. The response is to state a recommendation as a clear current choice under the available material, explaining its conditions, costs, opposing case, and revision points: derive what can be derived, verify what can be verified, and preserve boundaries where certification is unavailable. Trustworthy advice is not uncertainty-free; it does not hide uncertainty in fluent language. The value of AI-assisted analysis and authority for real-world execution can be judged separately, avoiding both overreach and abandonment of all grounded assistance merely because independent execution is unavailable.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First specify the task, intended conclusion, and action use, rather than assuming that every AI output has the same strength.

  2. 2

    Connect each of the eight material groups and AI selection and rewriting to the task, marking availability, absence, or reasoned inapplicability.

  3. 3

    Limit conclusions according to factual, causal, protective, and authorization dependencies, preserving unaffected local arguments.

  4. 4

    Give the current choice, key reasons, costs, strongest opposing case, and revision conditions, fully presenting the substantive analysis performed.

  5. 5

    Separate process validation from real-world evidence; check the respective authority for recommendations, formal adoption, and high-risk execution.

Distinctions to keep clear

Analytical recommendation

Provide a choice and reasons under the stated goals, premises, and material.

≠

Actual adoption and execution

Require authorized actors, normative procedures, and applicable protections.

Structural validation passes

Fields, types, or particular procedural constraints are satisfied.

≠

A real-world fact holds

Requires proportionate evidence about the object; form cannot validate itself.

Local evidence is missing

Blocks conclusions depending on that material.

≠

Uniform rejection of all analysis

Unaffected derivations, textual assessments, and conditional recommendations may hold.

Reasoned inapplicability

The item is genuinely unrelated to the bounded task, and the reason is given.

≠

Unknown or difficult to obtain

Inapplicability cannot be used to erase relevant risks.

Teaching construction: three conclusions in one reportTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe report, paragraphs, and indicators are teaching constructions; there are no real accident data.

Suppose a report contains Q1, “The source’s second paragraph has an unstated premise”; Q2, “The new process caused accidents to decline”; and Q3, “The institution has effectively protected feedback providers.” Reading the source may support Q1. Before-and-after accident totals without a proportionate causal design do not directly support Q2. Without material on protection against retaliation and independent review, Q3 cannot be certified. Restrictions on Q2 and Q3 do not automatically erase Q1; a correct Q1 does not endorse the other two either.

BoundaryEach conclusion still needs its own accuracy check. This example does not prove that before-and-after comparisons are never useful; it limits a particular causal claim.

Teaching construction: a correctly formatted false sourceTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe links and records are abstract constructions; no specific document that could be passed off as real has been fabricated.

An imagined JSON record contains correctly formatted source_url, title, and date fields, all of which pass validation. But if the link does not exist, or the page exists without the claimed fact, structural validation does not supply source authenticity or semantic support. The proper response is to retract the dependent factual assertion and complete verification, not add a declaration of “rigorous verification completed.”

BoundaryActual validation tools differ in capability; accurately state what the tool actually checked.

Conditional-recommendation construction: it may be proposed but not declared adoptedTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThis is an example of a design recommendation; no assessment, upload, or institutional process change was performed.

Under the public goal “reduce duplicate entry” and constraint “do not increase identity exposure,” AI may recommend first conducting an offline field-mapping assessment, listing costs and opposing arguments. If mapping is found to permit reidentification of rare roles, the recommendation should change. Without authorization, real sensitive data must not be uploaded, nor may the institution be said to have adopted the plan.

BoundaryThe feasibility and safety of the conditional recommendation still require proportionate material; protection cannot be described as already achieved.

A real judicial record: fabricated cases in Mata v. AviancaDocumented case

On June 22, 2023, the US District Court for the Southern District of New York recorded in its sanctions opinion in Mata v. Avianca that lawyers submitted AI-generated nonexistent cases and false quotations, and persisted after being challenged. Paragraph 6 of the Findings of Fact also records that the signatory checked style only and did not read the cited cases. The case makes concrete the distinction between reviewing prose style and verifying sources.

SourceMata v. Avianca，Opinion and Order on Sanctions，2023-06-22Opinion p1, opening paragraph; p4, Findings of Fact ¶6; p34, signature date. The document is hosted on the website of the US District Court for the District of ConnecticutReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThe guide uses the court’s original opinion only for the historical findings above. It does not claim to have read all 43 pages or reexamined the case file, offers no current legal advice, and does not estimate AI’s overall error rate from one case.

Read the case and sources

What counterexamples change

Teaching counterexampleThe validator says pass, so all facts, consent, and repair hold.

What it limitsThe validator covers only its actual rules and inputs; real-world conclusions require separate evidence.

Teaching counterexampleThere is no testimony from affected people, so even algebraic derivation under explicit assumptions cannot be discussed.

What it limitsCheck the relationship between testimony and the specific conclusion. Formal validity can be judged independently; do not silence discussion by counting missing items.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

Teaching counterexampleAI cannot be responsible for execution, so it should not recommend any choice.

What it limitsThe source allows grounded, refutable analytical recommendations; execution authority is checked separately.

Historical research manuscript: Xikari: On Conditions, Structure, and Transformation, source text supplied by the user

What does not follow

  • AI may offer grounded judgments, criticism, and recommendations, not just summaries; high-risk real-world decisions cannot be made independently.
  • Gaps in material and protection limit conclusions by dependence; a total count of gaps does not replace substantive judgment.
  • An appeal that upholds a correct decision may still be effective; do not demand a symbolic reversal to prove that appeals are useful.
  • Formal test results support only what was actually tested; artificial constructions must not be reported as real experiments.
  • This lesson has not verified the real-world safety of an AI system and offers no advice on specific litigation or high-impact action.

Scope and open questions

The original judicial text contains a clear record of source-verification failure, supporting the limited lesson that process review cannot replace factual verification.

  • No real AI-system stress test, inquiry into a commissioning party’s integrity, or verification of protective effects was conducted.
  • The case does not calibrate any AI model’s error rate; unverified material and output dependencies require separate judgments for each task.

  2. 2

  3. 3

  4. 4

    What must a current recommendation show at minimum?

If only one of three conclusions has independent evidence, should all pass or all be rejected?

Judge separately by dependence: retain the proportionately supported conclusion and limit the others. If a shared premise fails, explain the extent of the consequences.

How do we distinguish “the link exists” from “the fact has a source”?

Why does “not applicable” require a reason?

To prevent difficult evidence collection, unknowns, or real risks from being disguised as irrelevance; reasons should come from the relationship between task and conclusion.
