16.10GOV-10 Six Components of Weak-Signal Protection ​

In briefWillingness to hear a complaint is only a beginning. Whether information providers can enter safely, who receives their information, whether they are punished afterward, and whether the issue actually changes rules all determine whether “being heard” can lead to “being protected.”

Weak signals cannot depend only on a diagnostician being “willing to listen.” WEAK-SIGNAL-PROTECTION must register each of the following items.

WS1 Anonymous or low-exposure submission. People can submit facts without first disclosing their identity.

WS2 Independent parties to receive and take up the material. It must not go only to the chain of power being questioned.

WS3 Anti-retaliation records. Record loss of power, isolation, stigma, punishment, and changes in resources after feedback.

WS4 Calibration by group. Overall satisfaction or average performance must not hide deterioration among groups at the margins.

WS5 Delayed disclosure. When safety is at risk, protect those providing signals before discussing disclosure.

WS6 Evidence of write-back. After a signal is taken up, actual changes to rules, resources, responsibilities, or authoritative records must be visible.

If any component is missing, the output may say only that “the risk to weak signals has been recognized.” It must not claim that “weak signals have been protected.” One weak signal does not directly establish a conclusion. It also does not automatically disappear because it is infrequent, anonymous, emotional, or incomplete in form.

16.10Note

Understanding this section

16.10 GOV-10 Six-Part Protection for Weak Signals

Willingness to hear a complaint is only a beginning. Whether information providers can enter safely, who receives their information, whether they are punished afterward, and whether the issue actually changes rules all determine whether “being heard” can lead to “being protected.”

Weak signals are indications easily overlooked by mainstream records, averages, or positions of power. This section does not treat low frequency, anonymity, emotional expression, or incomplete formatting as automatic grounds for deletion. An indication cannot directly produce a final conclusion, but can identify facts and risks requiring checking. Responsibility for protection cannot be placed entirely on the speaker either: requiring a standardized report, public identity, and personally borne consequences before declaring a willingness to listen makes precisely what most needs visibility disappear first.

WS1 requires anonymous or low-exposure entry: submitting facts need not first expose identity. Assess actual usability, indirect identification, and control of materials, not merely whether a form has an anonymous option. Anonymity makes content neither inherently credible nor automatically invalid; checking can continue through factual indications and low-exposure methods. Collectors must also avoid recording task-irrelevant information merely to confirm identity.

WS2 requires an independent recipient who can take up the signal, not merely routing it to the challenged power chain. Changing the recipient’s job title does not guarantee independence: check funding, evaluation, control, interests, and whether they have appropriate capability and authority. Independent uptake does not permit arbitrary expansion of disclosure; information must be handled according to need and authorization so low-power providers are not identified through transfer. Receiving a report and having authority to change an institution are connected but distinct roles.

WS3’s anti-retaliation register tracks loss of authority, isolation, stigmatization, punishment, and resource changes after feedback. A promise of “no retaliation” is not actual protection; subsequent windows must allow changes to be detected and proportionate review and remedies arranged. Temporal proximity between a change and feedback is a clue, not automatic proof of retaliatory causation. Competing explanations and safe evidence gathering are required, while incomplete causal identification cannot justify ignoring grounded protective risks. Registration must not become another exposure of sensitive information.

WS4 requires group-level calibration so overall satisfaction or average performance does not conceal deterioration among marginalized groups. Grouping must relate to affected positions and the task, attending to sample size, opportunities to participate, and missingness mechanisms. Overall improvement cannot declare everyone better off, nor may disaggregation reidentify small groups. No universal fairness metric or threshold is supplied here; required groupings and publicly disclosable granularity depend on proportionate materials and protective conditions.

WS5 requires delayed disclosure: when safety risks exist, protect the provider before discussing publication. Connected to 16.6, delay does not mean hiding risk records forever; appropriate review, responsibility, and conditions are required. Review at expiry does not automatically disclose identity either. Verified bounded conclusions or handling outcomes may be disclosed in layers while original sensitive materials remain protected. Emergency protection and factual determinations must both respect applicable authority, not cross safety boundaries in the name of good intentions.

WS6 requires visible actual changes to rules, resources, responsibilities, or authoritative records after a signal is adopted. Receipts, summaries, meetings, or statements of “taking this very seriously” cannot substitute for change; change numbers must bind real versions and content. Accepting a fact does not mean accepting every recommendation, nor must every signal change an institution. Reasoned nonadoption requires a retained proportionate explanation; a symbolic one-word change cannot manufacture the appearance of feedback. Established actual change still differs from final net benefit or complete repair, which require outcome evidence separately.

All six items must be registered individually. If any is missing, one may say only that weak-signal risks have been recognized, not generally that weak signals have been protected. Completed local work can still be described truthfully—for example, an entry channel exists or independent uptake has occurred—but cannot stand for the entire protection package. Records for all six are not a permanent safety guarantee beyond actual verification; operation and consequences must be checked. The strongest objection says small teams cannot manage six elaborate items. Proportionate, low-burden arrangements are possible, but scarce resources cannot cancel key protections or transfer form-filling burdens to feedback providers already in low-power positions.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Retain low-frequency, anonymous, emotional, or incomplete indications, distinguishing risk entry from final factual conclusions.

  2. 2

    Check WS1 low-exposure entry, WS2 independent uptake, and WS3 follow-up anti-retaliation registration individually.

  3. 3

    Check WS4 group-level changes, preventing aggregate indicators from concealing marginalized harm and preventing reidentification of small groups.

  4. 4

    Check WS5 disclosure arrangements prioritizing safety and WS6 real write-back after adoption.

  5. 5

    Refuse overall protection certification if any item is missing, while truthfully retaining local work completed and materials still needed.

Distinctions to keep clear

Willingness to listen

A personal attitude or intention to provide entry.

≠

Protection implemented

All six responsibilities must be individually checkable, including subsequent consequences and write-back.

A single weak signal

An indication worth retaining and checking safely.

≠

A final factual conclusion

Requires proportionate evidence; one indication cannot automatically settle the case.

Improvement in the overall average

The aggregate indicator rises under stated weights and sample.

≠

Improvement at each affected position

Requires group-level checks; the whole cannot establish the result for every group.

Actual write-back after adoption

Rules, resources, responsibilities, or authoritative records actually change.

≠

Net benefit and complete repair

Still require evidence of outcomes, competing explanations, and related matters.

Mathematical construction: a rising average with deterioration at the marginsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsGroups, weights, scores, and complete observation are constructed assumptions; there is no real survey.

Assume a fixed 100 people on the same satisfaction scale from 0 to 100. Group A has 90 people whose mean rises from 70 to 80; group B has 10 whose mean falls from 60 to 40. The overall mean rises from (90×70+10×60)/100=69 to (90×80+10×40)/100=76: an increase of 7 points, while B falls by 20. Reporting only that 76 exceeds 69 misses the latter. The calculation demonstrates only the nonequivalence of averages and group-level results; it proves neither a real institution’s fairness nor causal harm to a group.

BoundaryReality also requires comparable measurement, treatment of missingness, and grounds for grouping; publishing small samples may reidentify people. This example is not a universal metric recommendation.

Teaching construction: after anonymous entryTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe organization and incident are constructed, not allegations against a real organization.

An imagined organization provides an anonymous mailbox but forwards original messages, including identifying job details, to the person complained about; afterward, no one records changes in the feedback provider’s shifts or resources. “An anonymous entry is open” cannot certify all six protections. First check actual exposure, independence of uptake, and subsequent protection; do not keep forcing more affected people to submit real-name materials to complete forms.

BoundaryWhether role details are identifying depends on context; removing names cannot be assumed sufficient for safety.

Teaching construction: write-back is content, not a receiptTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe member, rule, and change are teaching designs; no real institutional change was implemented.

An imagined member identifies an application rule that excludes those unable to attend at fixed times. After checking and adoption, there should be a verifiable new rule, usable alternative times, or corresponding responsibility arrangements. Merely sending “received” is not write-back. Even a changed rule cannot immediately establish that actual burdens disappeared; execution and subsequent materials from affected positions are still needed.

BoundaryReal recommendations may be rejected after reasoned review; changes cannot be manufactured for counting purposes.

Actual channel description: ASRS alerting messages and authority to actDocumented case

NASA ASRS’s Program Outputs page explains that reports of hazardous situations may lead to alerting messages to authorized parties for investigation and necessary corrective action. It also explicitly states that ASRS has no direct operational authority and must work through cooperation with others. This section adds a distinct observation: the website’s described alert-transfer mechanism does not prove that recipients completed institutional write-back.

What does not follow

  • The six items cannot replace one another; an anonymous mailbox does not also supply independence, protection against retaliation, and write-back.
  • One missing item prevents certification of overall protection, but should not conceal other verified local work.
  • Retaining weak signals is not immediately reaching a final conclusion; protecting providers does not require prior proof of all causation.
  • Grouping and follow-up registration must avoid additional exposure; do not collect irrelevant private information in the name of safety verification.
  • Substantive write-back does not require every opinion to change the result, nor allow minor edits to conceal key gaps.

Scope and open questions

An actual safety-report transfer mechanism shows that receipt, authority, and responsibility for actual correction differ; no report-induced change is invented.

  • Case-level anti-retaliation, group-level, and adoption write-back materials needed for full real-world certification of all six items are missing; this lesson makes no such certification.
  • No reader or institutional experiments were conducted; the teaching averages are not survey data.

Why does the example’s overall average rise while group B deteriorates?

With fixed weights, A’s larger positive contribution masks B’s decline. The overall mean moves from 69 to 76 and B from 60 to 40; both can be true simultaneously.

Basis: Weighted-mean calculation and group differences.

May an unconfirmed signal simply be deleted?

A signal cannot be deleted merely for being weak, anonymous, or emotional. Retain it as an indication and check it under safety and evidential conditions without immediately reaching a final conclusion.

How should independent receipt with no write-back evidence yet be reported?

Truthfully report receipt and verified local measures, identify gaps such as WS6, and do not claim all six protections are complete.

Does a rule update after adoption prove final repair?

It supports only the corresponding actual change; execution, burdens, and effects still require subsequent materials, without skipping levels.

16.11GOV-11 An Intermediate Path Without Institutional Infrastructure ​

In briefSmall teams, friends, and families may lack independent review and appeal bodies. Without those facilities, they should not pretend formal adjudication is complete; people can still record knowable facts, identify risks, and seek safer support without first risking themselves to prove who is absolutely wrong.

Families, intimate relationships, friendships, small teams, and temporary communities often lack independent reviewers, stable appeal procedures, and complete evidence chains. They can still involve ongoing harm, control of information, relational dependence, and risks to reputation or safety. NO-INFRASTRUCTURE-PATH does not simulate institutions that are absent, require people affected to take risks gathering evidence, or equate “cannot be reviewed” with “no facts can be recorded.”

It can output only a protective open assertion. State the current material, the continuing pattern that most warrants concern, prohibited uses, escalation signals, withdrawal signals, and a low-risk next step. The objective moves from “proving who is wrong” to reducing exposure, preserving records, restoring support, seeking an outside perspective, and observing subsequent signals. It must not be used for punishment, dossiers, eligibility decisions, public classification, or deprivation of resources.

16.11Note

Understanding this section

16.11 GOV-11 An intermediate path without institutional infrastructure

Small teams, friends, and families may lack independent review and appeal bodies. Without those facilities, they should not pretend formal adjudication is complete; people can still record knowable facts, identify risks, and seek safer support without first risking themselves to prove who is absolutely wrong.

NO-INFRASTRUCTURE-PATH applies to relational settings lacking independent reviewers, stable appeals, and complete evidence chains. Families, intimate relationships, friendships, small teams, and temporary communities may involve ongoing harm, information control, dependency, and reputational or safety risks, but inclusion among these types does not mean every relationship involves suppression. First state which facilities are actually missing and which materials and risks exist; relationship labels cannot replace investigation.

The intermediate path rejects two extremes: inventing an institution by calling oneself or the same power chain within the relationship an independent adjudicator, and claiming that no facts can be recorded because formal review is impossible. Specific events, parties’ statements, and preservable existing materials may be recorded separately with sources and uncertainties marked. Recording is not closure, and a record’s existence does not automatically prove an explanation of all events or motives. If gathering evidence increases exposure, affected people should not have to risk danger to earn belief.

The permitted output is a protective open assertion with six components fully developed. Current materials state what is actually known now, its sources, and gaps; the continuing pattern of greatest concern states recurring indications and competing explanations; prohibited uses make clear that this judgment cannot punish or deprive; escalation signals identify new facts that would make protection or external checking more urgent; withdrawal signals identify materials that would limit, revise, or withdraw the current explanation; low-risk next steps identify bounded actions to consider under existing safety and authority. Openness is not license to say anything: it retains conditions for changing the judgment and ceilings on use.

The action goal shifts from proving who is wrong to reducing exposure, preserving records, restoring support, seeking outside perspectives, and observing subsequent signals. Low risk must be judged relative to the specific context: an apparently ordinary screenshot, inquiry, public request for verification, or contact with family and friends may be monitored or escalate risk. Do not give everyone the same action list, still less recommend manipulating the other person, secretly accessing accounts, or deliberately provoking conflict to obtain evidence. If necessary, first reduce the details collected by this analysis rather than turn the person into research material.

This path cannot be used for punishment, dossiers, eligibility, public characterizations, or resource deprivation. “Preserving records” must be read together with “dossiers” among prohibited uses: safely retaining factual indications is not putting unresolved explanations into formal records used for evaluation, disciplinary action, or eligibility. Otherwise the two statements may be misread as simultaneously requiring and forbidding records. Subsequent formal disposition requires appropriate independent materials, grounds of authority, norms, and procedures; a protective open assertion cannot be directly upgraded into adjudication.

An outside perspective may help distinguish information and patterns, but any friend does not automatically qualify as an independent reviewer. Their ties to both parties, capability, confidentiality, and conflicts of interest must be considered. Accessing support does not authorize the supporter to decide for the person, nor mean support-seeking requires immediate departure, direct confrontation, or public disclosure. Connected to 16.12: inability to exit is not consent; protection should expand future choices rather than impose idealized action demands.

The strongest objection worries that open assertions are too weak to prevent real harm; another worries they enable unverified labels to spread. Both risks require limits on use. One may explicitly identify current facts as concerning and prioritize safety support while refusing verdicts on motives or public characterizations. When new external materials support or refute the account, revise the specific pattern and next steps; factual portions still grounded need not be erased. The intermediate path neither replaces formal emergency protection or lawful procedures nor certifies their existence; it avoids concealing missing infrastructure behind a fictitious complete institution.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Establish the actual conditions of existing review, appeal, and evidence chains; do not register nonexistent provisions as already available.

  2. 2

    Organize existing facts, statements, patterns, and unknowns separately, rejecting demands for risky evidence collection.

  3. 3

    Form protective open claims with all six components, clearly marking prohibited uses.

  4. 4

    Prioritize reducing exposure, connecting with support, and obtaining safe external perspectives, without making proof of who is right a prerequisite.

  5. 5

    Continue limiting judgments according to escalation and withdrawal signals; formal action must separately meet applicable grounds and procedures.

Distinctions to keep clear

No institutional infrastructure

Stable independent review, appeals, and similar arrangements are missing.

≠

Nothing is knowable

Local facts and risks may still be safely recorded; institutional absence cannot erase them all.

Protective open assertion

Specifies materials, patterns, ceilings on use, and conditions for changing the judgment.

≠

Public characterization

Fixes an unresolved explanation as a conclusion about a person; this path does not authorize it.

Preserving existing records

Safely retaining knowable facts and indications.

≠

Disciplinary or eligibility dossiers

Using unresolved assertions as formal grounds for evaluation or deprivation: a prohibited use.

Low-risk next steps

Proceed in a bounded way according to specific exposure and permission conditions.

≠

Uniform evidence-collection checklist

Requiring screenshots, confrontation, or disclosure regardless of context may increase risk.

Teaching construction: how to write a six-part open claimTeaching scenario

AssumptionsAll people, messages, and circumstances are constructed; no interviews or investigation were conducted.

Suppose a temporary collaboration group has no independent appeal. Current materials: two received messages changing tasks and a personal diary, but no complete correspondence. Pattern warranting attention: repeated task changes may impose extra workload on one member; motives cannot yet be judged. Prohibited uses: no public labeling, punishment, or disqualification on this basis. Escalation signals: new verifiable threats, withdrawal of support, or continued workload increases. Withdrawal signals: independent materials show that the original messages included an omitted negotiation process, requiring revision of the pattern judgment. Low-risk next step: when the person’s safety and wishes allow, first organize existing materials and consider a trusted external perspective, without creating conflict to obtain more evidence.

Boundary“Two messages” does not establish a persistent pattern; do not declare the next step certainly safe when actual safety conditions are unknown.

Teaching construction: preservation differs from a disciplinary fileTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThis illustrates a use boundary; no real private information was retained or sent.

Suppose a member, when safety permits, retains messages they have already received and notes dates and uncertainties; this preserves leads. Another person turns those fragments into a permanent personnel file stating “this person cannot be worked with” and forwards it to recruiters; this exceeds the use ceiling of protective open claims and cannot be justified as “keeping a record.”

BoundaryActual recording and transmission must still comply with applicable privacy, authorization, and safety requirements; this example does not provide legal advice.

Teaching construction: absence of review does not erase local factsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe notice and agreement are conditional assumptions.

Suppose a verifiable notice explicitly cancels an agreed form of support; the fact of that notice can hold. Whether it constitutes intentional isolation, overall control, or breach of contract requires other materials and procedures. The middle path permits retaining the notice and recording risks, but does not permit claiming the notice never existed because other evidence is missing, or directly finding guilt.

BoundaryMultiple interpretations may be possible in reality; a local fact neither automatically obtains an overall interpretation nor is negated by an unresolved overall judgment.

A real support guide: consider safety before documentingDocumented case

NNEDV Safety Net’s guide to documenting technology abuse states that existing materials may still be useful even if they do not meet best-practice documentation formats; it also warns that discovery of documentation may lead to escalation, so safety should come first. When listing possible methods, the guide also says that an item’s appearance on the list does not establish that it is happening in a particular reader’s situation.

SourceNNEDV Safety Net Project, webpage copyright 2025Documentation Tips, introductory paragraph and Think about your safety first item; What might I want to document?, first paragraphReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis is guide text published by a support organization, not a real personal case or an effectiveness trial; this lesson does not confirm victimization or surveillance for any particular reader or prescribe evidence-collection actions.

What it limitsInstitutional deficiencies limit strong conclusions but do not erase knowable facts and risks.

Teaching counterexampleBecause the purpose is protection, unverified interpretations may be made public to everyone.

What it limitsThe original rejects requiring affected people to collect evidence at personal risk; support should not come at the cost of continued exposure.

What does not follow

  • The type of relationship does not establish ongoing harm; facts and interpretations must be distinguished using current materials.
  • The absence of formal review does not make all facts unrecordable, nor does it permit one to appoint oneself judge.
  • Protective open claims must not be used for punishment, formal personnel records, eligibility, public characterization, or deprivation of resources.
  • Do not require risky evidence collection, direct confrontation, or immediate exit; low risk must be assessed against actual safety conditions.
  • This lesson is textual research; it does not diagnose risks in, or give action instructions for, the reader’s or any real relationship.

Scope and open questions

Real support-practice literature directly addresses documentation quality, contextual judgment, and prioritizing safety, providing material for bounded support where institutions are insufficient.

  • No factual investigation of any real family, small team, or relationship was conducted.
  • No materials suffice to certify a specific next step as safe; the guide cannot replace judgment of an individual situation.

A provisional interpretation can too easily become permanently fixed as correct; specify what materials would lead to revision or withdrawal, and retain versions.

No. Safe documentation and use for disciplinary eligibility are different; the latter is outside this path’s authority.

Not automatically. An external perspective has local value, but relationships, competence, confidentiality, and authority must be considered.

Screenshots, public inquiries, and contacting supporters can all increase exposure in particular circumstances; they must be bounded by safety and the person’s wishes.

16.12GOV-12 Protection of Subjects Unable to Exit ​

In briefA person may remain in a relationship or arrangement because they have nowhere feasible to go, care cannot be interrupted, or their income is controlled—not because they agree to everything happening. Protection should first reduce harm and preserve choices, without requiring “successful departure” as proof that they deserve support.
Codes used in this section (1)
  • M07Delegation/Representation

Children, people with severe dependencies, people whose income sources are controlled, incarcerated people, people bound to care arrangements, or people with extremely limited resources may be unable to exit. Remaining does not amount to consent. INABILITY-TO-EXIT-PROTECTION requires six safeguards: prioritize safety, provide trusted representatives, restore minimal choices, information, records, and connections to support, keep records with low exposure, provide local buffers and alternative ways out, and prohibit romanticizing inability to exit as love, loyalty, maturity, sacrifice, or service to the larger interest.

People should not have to remain exposed to prove their circumstances. Allow submission through a representative, delayed expression, phased disclosure, outside arrangements to take over, preservation of evidence, and refusal of direct dialogue. The objective of protection under conditions that prevent exit is to reduce harm, preserve subjecthood, and expand future choices. An ideal exit must not be forced.

The tasks taken on by a trusted representative must be specified. Record the grounds and scope separately for assisting understanding and expression, submitting materials for someone, handling a matter delegated by the person, and making a decision on the person’s behalf. A representative’s statement cannot automatically be recorded as the person’s own expression or consent. Preserve means of communication the person can use, conflicts of interest, conditions for refusing or changing support, review of objections, and continuity of necessary support. If the person’s wishes remain unclear, state the support efforts made, grounds for interpretation, and uncertainty. Substitute decisions and emergency measures in records or institutions also require separate checks on their institutional basis and normative disputes. Kinship, professional qualifications, or convenience of representation do not establish full standing to represent. Recording requirements must not be used to interrupt necessary support or force disclosure. See the Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, General Comment No. 1 (2014) and its 2018 corrigendum. For representation and authorization, see M07 and D.21.

16.12Note

Understanding this section

16.12 GOV-12 Protecting Subjects Who Cannot Exit

A person may remain in a relationship or arrangement because they have nowhere feasible to go, care cannot be interrupted, or their income is controlled—not because they agree to everything happening. Protection should first reduce harm and preserve choices, without requiring “successful departure” as proof that they deserve support.

Original location: Chinese source lines 3646–3653; original anchor section-16-12; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Not exiting does not equal consent.” A verbatim source excerpt for this topic is separately attached in source-slice.md, keeping explanation apart from the original.

This section lists children, severely dependent people, people whose income is controlled, incarcerated people, people bound by care responsibilities, and subjects with extremely limited resources, noting that they may be unable to exit. This identifies a possibility and an entry point for protection; it does not presume from identity that everyone lacks will or capacity. Exit depends on affordable costs, continuity of support, information, real options, and safety; nominal permission to leave that entails losing necessary care is not feasible exit. Remaining cannot automatically be interpreted as consent, loyalty, or approval of the arrangement.

The six protections are: safety first; trusted proxies; restoration of minimal choice, information, records, and connections to support; low-exposure documentation; local buffers and alternative exits; and prohibiting romanticization of inability to exit as love, loyalty, maturity, sacrifice, or the greater good. They are not six tests for the person to pass, but responsibilities of protective arrangements. Minimal choice may mean an available communication channel, saying no to one step, or a temporary buffer; its value cannot be denied because a complete exit plan is not yet available. Yet small choices must not conceal ongoing restrictions.

People should not be required to remain exposed to prove their situation. The original allows proxy submission, delayed expression, staged disclosure, external uptake, preservation of evidence, and refusal of direct dialogue. Allowing these methods does not declare every method safe in every context, authorized, or legally effective; actual exposure and support conditions must be examined. In particular, “dialogue can solve the problem” must not become a rule forcing someone to face the person being questioned, nor may refusal of dialogue be rewritten as noncooperation.

The goal is to reduce harm, preserve agency, and expand future options under conditions where exit is impossible, rather than force an ideal exit. If moving now would interrupt necessary care or increase danger, first check alternative uptake arrangements and buffers; external support can help expand the conditions available and should not require immediate departure as a prerequisite for help. This connects to the boundaries of X0 and transfer to external uptake: leaving the nominal old environment does not automatically provide safety, support for living, or continuity of responsibility. Protection must not rationalize long-term entrapment either; feasible choices still need to be sought continuously.

Trusted proxies must distinguish four kinds of work by matter: helping a person understand and express themselves, submitting materials on their behalf, handling matters entrusted by them, and making decisions on their behalf. The first two do not automatically include the latter two, and an authorization for one matter does not expand into representation in every domain. Record the grounds, scope, and limits separately; a proxy’s account cannot automatically be written as the person’s own expression or consent. Relatives, professionals, and familiar caregivers may provide important support, but neither identity nor convenience is sufficient standing to represent someone.

Also preserve the person’s available ways of communicating, records of proxy conflicts of interest, conditions for refusing or changing support, review of dissent, and continuity of necessary support. Communication may differ from a formal spoken answer; expression cannot be erased merely because it does not fit a conventional form, nor can a supporter’s guess be passed off as the person’s own words. Changing support should not suddenly interrupt necessities for living, and imperfect records cannot become an excuse to force disclosure or stop necessary support.

If the person’s wishes remain indeterminate after support, state what support efforts were made, the grounds of interpretation, and the remaining uncertainty. “I cannot understand” cannot directly be registered as “the person has no will,” nor may a result be decided first and a proxy statement then sought as consent. Where materials or institutions contain substitute decision-making and emergency measures, check their institutional grounds and normative disputes separately; describing what an institution permits does not establish conformity with this section’s protective principles, still less authorize issuing permission for real people on the basis of this book.

The strongest opposing position emphasizes that, when information and communication are limited and support cannot wait, making no arrangements at all may also harm people. This difficulty requires distinguishing uninterrupted necessary support, revocable bounded arrangements, cautious interpretation of wishes, and actual substitute decision-making, while retaining corresponding grounds, review, and disputes; urgency cannot expand proxy authority without limit. Another objection worries that all proxies are being deemed untrustworthy. This section makes no such presumption; it requires verifiable scope, conflicts of interest, and conditions for the person to change support, so that trustworthiness is more than a self-description.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Check actual exit conditions; do not treat staying or an identity category as proof of consent or incapacity.

  2. 2

    Implement the six protections, prioritizing reduced exposure and continuity of necessary support.

  3. 3

    Distinguish support, submission, entrusted handling, and substitute decision-making by the four kinds of matter, recording their respective grounds and boundaries.

  4. 4

    Preserve the person’s communication, conflict-of-interest records, refusal and changes of support, and review of dissent, preventing proxies from overriding the person.

  5. 5

    When wishes are unclear, report support efforts, interpretive grounds, and unknowns; substitute decision-making and emergency measures require separate institutional and normative checks, and do not automatically obtain sufficient authorization.

Distinctions to keep clear

Inability to exit

Real options, resources, safety, or other conditions make departure infeasible.

≠

Consent to continue

Requires corresponding expression, information, and conditions; it cannot be presumed from staying.

Support for understanding and expression

Helps the person form and express judgments.

≠

Substitute decision-making

Hands decisions to another person; grounds and normative disputes require separate checking.

Proxy statement

An account made by the proxy on the basis of their materials and understanding.

≠

The person’s own expression or consent

Must not be replaced directly without distinction.

Continuity of necessary support

Protects basic living and communication conditions from interruption.

≠

Unconditional continuation of proxy control

Continuity of support does not mean a proxy can never be changed.

Teaching construction: submission on someone’s behalf is not consent on their behalfTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe people, feedback, and picture cards are all teaching assumptions; no real care decision is involved.

Suppose a care-service user asks a supporter to submit feedback about daily routines to the service provider. The supporter may submit that matter, but cannot also sign consent to relocation or declare that the person waives an appeal. If the person uses picture cards to express a wish to change one arrangement, preserve the communication materials and context, rather than treating the supporter’s full retelling as a verbatim quotation.

BoundaryThe effect of a particular delegation or consent must be checked separately against actual institutions, norms, and the person’s expression; this example issues no authorization.

Teaching construction: changing support must not interrupt supportTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe situation is constructed; no service adjustment was implemented.

Suppose someone wants to replace a helper with a conflict of interest, but still relies on that helper’s services for daily communication. Proportionate protection requires alternative communication and service continuity, rather than saying “if you reject this person, all support is cancelled.” Conversely, the importance of the service cannot justify permanently locking in the same proxy.

BoundaryWhether replacement resources are actually available needs checking; verbal promises cannot establish safety.

Teaching construction: multiple explanations for stayingTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe home, member, and resource conditions are all hypothetical.

Suppose a member still lives at the same address: they may prefer to stay, or they may lack financial resources or alternative care. Unchanged residence alone cannot distinguish these possibilities. Protective records should list existing materials, feasible choices, and unknowns; “they did not leave” cannot establish consent, still less justify forcing immediate relocation to complete the proof.

BoundaryNo blanket finding of control is made about any real co-residential or dependent relationship.

A real normative text and corrigendum: support is not substitute decision-makingDocumented case

The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities’ 2014 General Comment No. 1 discusses respect for will, communication support, and safeguards in support relationships in paragraphs 17, 21, and 29. The corrigendum of January 26, 2018, replaces paragraph 27, using “or,” rather than the original “and,” when listing characteristics of substitute decision-making regimes. Interpreters must therefore check versions and cannot mistakenly require all three characteristics simultaneously as the only identification condition.

16.13GOV-13 Complex Trauma and the Absence of a Healthy Baseline ​

In brief“Restoring things as they were” sounds like repair, but the earlier state may never have been safe. Where a healthy baseline is absent, first ask how minimum safety and predictable support can be established today; do not invent an ideal past for someone to fit a repair narrative.

Some structures have never had a healthy state. First distinguish structures that departed from a healthier state, structures with a nominal anchor that has hollowed out in practice, newly formed structures that never developed a healthy anchor, and structures whose rules, identities, boundaries, and relations were formed through trauma.

For the latter two, TRAUMA-NO-HEALTHY-BASELINE asks what minimum safety means now, whether the subject is receiving predictable support for the first time, whether they can express themselves without punishment, whether small instances of trust can be repeated, which survival strategies previously protected them but are becoming constraints, and whether a new anchor can be found or must be built together. It does not ask “how to get back to the original state.”

Treatment, clinical care, caregiving, child protection, or legal tasks requiring particular qualifications should be handled under the corresponding professional procedures. Expertise and credentials do not confer authority over the whole of someone’s life. Goals the person values, communication they can understand, objections, and refusal must still be addressed in the relevant procedure. Emergency duties and authority over particular matters require independent grounds that apply to the case. The framework cannot infer them into existence. State scope, validity period, review, and continuity of support separately. The framework cannot use its theory to invent a healthy past. See §1.3, §2.8, and §14.2 for limits on authority, and §15.3.8 for emergency tasks.

“Trauma-built” is a candidate description of the formation history of some structures. It does not designate complex post-traumatic stress disorder or another clinical diagnosis. Harm that calls for protection now can be recorded first. The formation history, particular psychological mechanisms, and professional classification each need evidence. Present harm cannot be used to infer that every relationship was formed by trauma. People do not have to establish that an ideal past once existed to receive support.

16.13Note

Understanding this section

16.13 GOV-13 Complex Trauma and the Absence of a Healthy Baseline

“Restoring things as they were” sounds like repair, but the earlier state may never have been safe. Where a healthy baseline is absent, first ask how minimum safety and predictable support can be established today; do not invent an ideal past for someone to fit a repair narrative.

Original location: Chinese source lines 3654–3663; original anchor section-16-13; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “The framework cannot use its own theory to invent a healthy past.” A verbatim source excerpt for this topic is separately attached in source-slice.md, keeping explanation apart from the original.

This section first distinguishes four structural histories: a formerly healthier structure that later departed from that state; a nominal anchor that remains but is hollow in practice; an initial-building type in which a healthy anchor never formed; and a trauma-as-building-material type in which rules, identities, boundaries, and relationships formed under traumatic conditions from the outset. They point to different questions: grounded restoration, checking the gap between nominal and actual conditions, establishing conditions for the first time, or reexamining constraints embedded during formation. These four are neither a list of clinical diagnoses nor stages every object must pass through.

A healthier past requires historical evidence; it cannot be inferred solely from “things later became worse.” Even a surviving nominal anchor requires checking current uptake and effects; institutional names or old slogans do not establish continued operation. Both the initial-building and trauma-as-building-material types may lack a healthy state to return to, but they are not identical: not yet having formed does not automatically establish formation through harm, and current behavior cannot substitute for formation history.

For the latter two types, TRAUMA-NO-HEALTHY-BASELINE does not default to returning to the original state; instead it asks in six directions: current minimum safety; whether predictable support is being obtained for the first time; whether expression is possible without punishment; whether small, repeatable trust is available; which strategies once protected survival but now constrain it; and whether new anchors already exist but remain unseen or need to be built together. These questions must connect with the person and specific conditions, rather than define one standard healthy life for everyone.

Predictable support centers on repeatedly dependable conditions, not a single intense promise; an unpunished entry point centers on actual consequences, not merely saying expression is allowed; small, repeatable trust also cannot be produced by forced disclosure, demands for forgiveness, or direct confrontation. Strategies that once protected someone should not casually be dismissed as defects, while whether they now restrict choices can still be discussed through specific materials. This explains research directions; it prescribes no treatment steps and guarantees no effects for anyone.

Discovering new anchors differs from building them together. Discovery requires evidence of existing relationships, commitments, or support; construction is new negotiation and practice, requiring records of participants’ goals, boundaries, conditions for withdrawal, and actual consequences. An analyst’s preferred values cannot be declared the object’s true anchors, nor can minimum safety now be denied because a goal has not formed. “Building together” must not obscure power differences: who has resources, who can refuse, and who bears costs still need checking.

Tasks requiring corresponding qualifications—such as therapy, clinical work, care, child protection, and law—should go through the relevant professional procedures. Framework research cannot itself issue clinical classifications, treatment plans, guardianship arrangements, or legal judgments. Professional knowledge and credentials likewise do not create power to decide every aspect of a person’s life: the person’s valued goals, comprehensible communication, dissent, and refusal still require handling through applicable procedures. Emergency duties and authority over specific matters need independently applicable grounds; explain scope, duration, review, and continuity of support separately, rather than deriving “I understand, therefore I have authority” from theory.

“Trauma-as-building-material type” is only a candidate description of certain structural formation histories, not complex post-traumatic stress disorder or another clinical diagnosis. Present harm requiring protection may be recorded first; formation history, psychological mechanisms, and professional classifications carry separate evidentiary responsibilities. Being harmed today does not imply that all past relationships were constituted by trauma; incomplete history does not require suspending all safety support. Nor must people prove they once had an ideal past to qualify for help.

The strongest opposing position worries that rejecting a healthy baseline makes improvement arbitrary, allowing any new arrangement to be called repair. The response is not to fabricate a past, but to clarify present minimum safety, the person’s goals, normative boundaries, testable improvement, and counterexamples, distinguishing protection, initial construction, and evidence-based restoration. Another objection worries that “it once protected survival” exempts present restrictions from examination; acknowledging a historical function does not mean keeping it forever, and current costs, alternative conditions, and the person’s feasible choices can still be evaluated.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    Check the four candidate explanations of structural history separately; do not infer a healthy or traumatic past from current harm.

  2. 2

    Without a healthy baseline, turn to questions of minimum safety, predictable support, expression, small trust, survival strategies, and new anchors.

  3. 3

    Distinguish discovery of existing conditions from jointly building new ones, retaining the person’s goals and refusal.

  4. 4

    Collect evidence separately for current harm, formation history, psychological mechanisms, and clinical classifications; none replaces another.

  5. 5

    Tasks requiring professional qualifications enter the corresponding procedures; credentials and urgency do not automatically expand authority over matters.

Distinctions to keep clear

Repairing previously healthier conditions

Use real historical and current functional evidence to determine what should be restored.

≠

Building safe support for the first time

The corresponding baseline may never have existed; do not pretend this is a return.

Trauma-as-building-material type

A candidate description of structural formation history.

≠

Clinical diagnosis

Requires corresponding professional evidence and procedures, not an inference from a framework label.

A strategy once had a protective effect

Describes its bounded function under conditions at the time.

≠

It should still be retained now

Current costs and alternatives require a separate judgment.

Professional competence

Knowledge and qualifications to undertake specific tasks.

≠

Power to decide all aspects of life

Still requires authority over the matter, the person’s goals, and procedures; credentials do not confer unlimited authority.

Teaching construction: four histories cannot all be called restorationTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe four groups and histories are teaching constructions; no real organization was assessed.

Suppose mutual-aid group A once had verifiable safe expression and resource support that later stopped; B nominally retains a support committee but accepts nothing in practice; C has just formed and has not yet developed stable support; D’s rules have been built around punitive control from the start. A may study which existing conditions to restore; B checks hollowing out; C needs initial construction; D checks formation history and how to rebuild safer arrangements. The same goal of “returning to the original state” cannot handle all four.

BoundaryReal situations may be mixed, contain conflicting evidence, or remain unknown; they cannot be forcibly classified by resemblance to a story.

Teaching construction: old strategies and new conditionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA conditional strategy example; no psychological mechanism was judged for a real person.

Suppose a member has long avoided conflict by not expressing needs, which may have protected them at the time; after entering a hypothetically safer environment, it may also restrict access to help. Analysis should ask whether current expression is truly safe and whether alternative support exists, rather than ordering immediate disclosure of every experience or diagnosing silence as a disease.

BoundaryBoth historical protection and current restriction require facts; this pattern cannot be imposed on everyone who is silent.

Teaching construction: qualifications still have boundariesTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA construction about authority relationships; no instructions for any real emergency action are provided.

Suppose a professional may conduct a specific commissioned assessment, but cannot therefore decide all of the person’s friends, interests, and life goals. If an emergency arises, independently applicable grounds, time limits, review, and continuity of support still need checking; a theory calling something “dangerous” cannot justify self-expansion of authority.

BoundaryActual clinical and legal authority depends on professional procedures and local rules, not this example.

A real public-health definition: division of responsibilities between trauma-informed practice and specialist treatmentDocumented case

The UK government’s working definition published on November 2, 2022, emphasizes safety, trust, choice, and collaboration; the “Prevent re-traumatisation” section explicitly states that trauma-informed practice focuses on reducing barriers to services, while treatment of trauma-related difficulties is undertaken by specialist services and staff. This provides a real normative text that does not equate service design directly with treatment.

SourceGOV.UK，Working definition of trauma-informed practice，2022-11-02Publication date; Prevent re-traumatisation, paragraph 2; Key principles subsections Safety, Trustworthiness, Choice, and CollaborationReading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsThis text does not validate Xikari’s trauma-as-building-material type or establish the effectiveness of a particular service; this lesson does not convert guiding principles into personal diagnosis or treatment advice.

What it limitsA past baseline needs evidence; without one, initial construction rather than restoration may be needed.

What does not follow

  • Do not invent a healthy past or assume that all formation history was constituted by trauma because harm exists now.

  • Do not conflate initial-building and trauma-as-building-material types or treat the four categories as a developmental sequence.

Scope and open questions

A real professional guidance text illustrates responsibility boundaries between supportive environments and specialist treatment, without inventing clinical cases.

  • No healthy baseline or traumatic formation history was established for any real object.
  • No treatment effect was tested; current harm, formation mechanisms, and clinical classifications each require their own materials.

16.14GOV-14 Keeping Open-Ended Undertaking, Normative Premises, and Metaphorical Drift Separate ​

In briefWhether someone is willing to bear costs, whether it helps, and whether we should praise it are three questions. A good result does not establish that they acted voluntarily, nor does sincerity guarantee a beneficial outcome; still less may everything unexplained be called love.
Codes used in this section (2)
  • HV11Open-Ended Undertaking
  • G2Specified-Channel Effects and Per-Dimension Boundedness

Love must not be treated as “the remainder that structure cannot explain” or as a favored label for a motive. A description of bounded voluntary undertaking uses HV11-R1-voluntary-limited-action. First check the action, identifiable costs, direction, voluntariness, and genuine conditions for refusal, exit, or negotiation. Also check competing explanations such as interests, fear, benefits of identity, inertia, dependence, and coercion. The result can be achieved, unrealized, harmful, or unknown. Successful structural consequences are not an entry requirement for R1. Failed attempts must not disappear by definition.

A causal judgment about structural consequences uses HV11-R2-structural-consequence. Whether the action changes safety, the ability to refuse, appeal, resources, or later possibilities for affected positions must be judged separately under the relevant G2/causal contract. A beneficial result cannot establish voluntariness retroactively. Sincerity and high costs cannot substitute for evidence of effects. Normative approval of the action also requires disclosure of the N premises adopted, the protection floor, and costs to others affected. Whether the description holds, whether the effect holds, and whether the action deserves approval are questions that can each be answered affirmatively or negatively. Risks identified by R0 can generate requirements for protection directly without waiting for R1 or R2 to receive support.

These routes constrain the framework’s judgments about particular undertakings and their consequences. They do not exhaust the meaning of love, care, or goodwill in general. Kindness at low cost, private companionship, creative attempts that did not succeed, and the value of ordinary relationships can matter in the appropriate context. Failure to meet a route’s conditions does not negate the actor’s inner life or personality. Voluntarily bearing a limited cost does not create an unlimited duty to continue. Necessary arrangements for others to take over and release from responsibility must be justified separately for the matter at hand.

A broad utility representation can incorporate concern for others, identity, or commitments. Representing a choice as optimal does not by itself identify the reasons for acting or replace a judgment about its normative standing (see Sen, 1977). Filling in benefits after seeing choices so that any outcome becomes optimal cannot distinguish competing explanations. Exploratory extensions can be retained. A claim of new explanatory capability must state which outcomes the new model can distinguish relative to the old one, on what grounds, and what materials would make the explanation fail. See §2.4 and D.15.

Normative premises must be disclosed and referred to Part 14. The framework openly commits to protecting subjects with little power and rejecting uses of structural language that erase responsibility. It favors access to appeal and withdrawal and the continued development of successors able to take up the work. They do not follow automatically from facts as neutral conclusions.

The status of a concept used across domains must be marked as metaphor, analogy, candidate mechanism, corroborating empirical evidence, formal model, or verified rule. “Resembles” must not be rewritten as “follows.” Cases from physics, biology, or animal behavior do not directly establish conclusions about human organizations or institutions. Each metaphor must specify similarities, differences, risks of misuse, and evidence that would lead to stopping its use.

16.14Note

Understanding this section

16.14 GOV-14 Separating Open-Ended Undertaking, Normative Premises, and Metaphorical Drift

Whether someone is willing to bear costs, whether it helps, and whether we should praise it are three questions. A good result does not establish that they acted voluntarily, nor does sincerity guarantee a beneficial outcome; still less may everything unexplained be called love.

Original location: Chinese source lines 3664–3677; original anchor section-16-14; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Whether a description holds, an effect holds, and something deserves praise are three questions that can each receive an affirmative or negative answer.” A verbatim source excerpt for this topic is separately attached in source-slice.md, keeping explanation apart from the original.

This section treats love neither as a residual left unexplained by structure nor as an a priori motive label. HV11-R1-voluntary-limited-action describes only bounded voluntary undertaking: check the action, identifiable costs, direction, voluntariness, and actual conditions for refusal, exit, or negotiation, while examining competing explanations such as interests, fear, identity benefits, inertia, dependency, and coercion. Costs may be distributed across positions; do not see only the actor’s apparent contribution while ignoring burdens borne by others. Competing explanations do not mean denying goodwill in advance; they prevent a favored story from replacing materials.

R1 allows outcomes to be achieved, unachieved, harmful, or unknown; successful structural consequences are not an entry condition. If an action has evidence of voluntariness and bounded costs, failure must not erase the attempt by definition; conversely, a coerced action cannot be retrospectively made voluntary because it produced good outcomes. A clear direction does not equal a justified direction; descriptive facts and normative praise must still be stated separately.

HV11-R2-structural-consequence judges whether an action, through specified channels, changes affected positions’ safety, ability to refuse, appeals, resources, or subsequent possibilities. It must follow the corresponding G2/causal contract and check CAUSAL and E4 under the HV11 card (source theory-hv11, A.11, Chinese source line 4674). Before-and-after change does not automatically identify causation, and sincerity or high costs cannot replace effect evidence. R2 is not a second stage requiring prior R1: coerced actions may also have identifiable structural effects, and an affirmative R2 still does not supply R1 voluntariness.

Normative approval separately discloses N premises, the protection floor, and costs to other affected people. An objective may improve one indicator while sacrificing others' right to refuse; whether it merits approval cannot be assessed solely by the net total or the actor's wishes. Protecting low-power actors, opposing the cancellation of responsibility through structural language, and favoring appeal, withdrawal, and reproduction of those able to take up the work are value boundaries the framework explicitly undertakes. They belong in Part Fourteen, rather than being disguised as neutral theorems automatically derived from facts.

Action costs, coercion, or gaps in stopping rights revealed by R0 can directly establish protection needs without waiting for voluntariness and causal effects to be fully confirmed. Here, “establishing needs” does not mean the framework acquires power to implement protection or redistribute resources itself; actual action still requires corresponding authority, procedures, and risk conditions. Nor may failure to meet R1 negate personhood or inner worth, or satisfaction of R1 justify demanding continued sacrifice until the task ends. A bounded undertaking does not automatically generate unlimited obligations; necessary continuity and release from responsibility require separate reasoning for the matter.

These routes do not exhaust love, care, or general goodwill. Low-cost kindness, private companionship, unsuccessful creativity, and the value of everyday relations can hold in appropriate contexts. Greater cost must not be equated with deeper love, nor may the existence of G2 causal identification judge all private meaning. Here the framework limits only how strong its judgments can be about specific undertakings and consequences; it does not monopolize every use of these words.

Broad utility can incorporate concern, identity, and commitment, so utility theory cannot simply be said to permit only narrow self-interest. But representing an observed choice as optimal under some utility function does not independently identify the actual reason or determine its normative standing. If every observed choice is retroactively assigned the highest payoff, the model can fit any outcome but cannot distinguish competing explanations such as interest, fear, or commitment. Exploratory extensions may be retained, but a claim of increased explanatory power must specify which additional possible outcomes are distinguished relative to the original model, on what grounds, and what material would make the explanation fail.

Cross-domain concepts require six identities to be marked: metaphors aid expression; analogies compare bounded relations; candidate mechanisms propose channels for testing; empirical corroboration supplies bounded external material; formal models derive results under explicit assumptions; and validated rules may be used only within their actual validation scope. These six are not labels that can be upgraded merely by polishing language. Something being “like” another system does not mean it “follows” that system's laws; material from physics, biology, or animal behavior does not directly establish conclusions about human institutions.

Each metaphor should state similarities, differences, risks of misuse, and evidence for discontinuing it. For example, “a team is like an immune system” may prompt attention to detecting and responding to anomalies, but members have meanings, rights, dissent, and exit; dissenters cannot be eliminated as pathogens. If the analogy begins concealing these differences or fails to yield new distinguishable questions, discontinue or narrow it rather than using natural phenomena to justify organizational sanctions.

The strongest objection is that separating action, effect, and norms so finely makes everyday goodwill impossible to express. The response is to preserve expressive space in different contexts while clarifying the material required for strong assertions; not all care needs a causal trial. Another objection says that any choice can be represented through utility, so no other explanation is needed. Representability does not mean the cause has been identified. If different explanations have exactly the same predictions and evidence, acknowledge that they remain undistinguished rather than declaring a winner through repeated renaming.

How the argument develops

  1. 1

    First check R0 action costs and risks; do not wait for a complete positive route before recognizing protection needs.

  2. 2

    For R1, separately check action, cost, direction, voluntariness, and genuine refusal, exit, and negotiation; retain failed and unknown outcomes.

  3. 3

    For R2, use a proportionate causal contract to judge specified structural consequences; effects must not fill in motives or voluntariness.

  4. 4

    Normative approval discloses N premises, the protection floor, and costs to others; authority for actual action is checked separately.

  5. 5

    Utility representations require discriminating power and failure conditions; cross-domain uses must mark their identity, similarities, differences, risks, and evidence for discontinuation.

Distinctions to keep clear

R1 bounded voluntary undertaking

An evidenced description of action; its outcome may fail or remain unknown.

≠

R2 structural causal consequences

An effect judgment for specified channels, objects, and windows; it cannot disprove or supply missing evidence of voluntariness.

Beneficial effect

One possible answer concerning outcomes and causal support.

≠

Deserving approval

Separately requires public value premises and costs to affected people.

A choice is representable as optimal

Some utility representation exists.

≠

The reason for action has been identified

Requires distinguishing competing explanations, not retroactive filling-in.

Metaphor or analogy

Bounded similarities help formulate questions.

≠

A validated rule for human institutions

Requires independent bridging and object evidence; it cannot be inferred directly from natural systems.

Teaching construction: different answers to three questionsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsPeople, durations, and evidence conditions are hypothetical; no actual work-effect experiment was conducted.

Suppose A can freely refuse and explicitly agrees to undertake two hours of work to help a colleague, but the method is ineffective. R1's bounded voluntary action can hold while an R2 beneficial effect remains unsupported. B performs the same work under threat, and independent evidence does show improved outcomes: R2 may hold while R1 does not. Whether the arrangements merit approval still requires value premises and costs to others; B's good output cannot justify approving coercion.

BoundaryActual R2 must meet the corresponding contract. The story's “independent evidence” is a conditional premise, not something this lesson has verified.

Mathematical construction: why retroactive payoffs do not identify reasonsTeaching scenario

AssumptionsThe two options and numbers form a formal construction; they estimate no real person's utility.

Let the choice set be A={a,b}. Defining u(a)=1 and u(b)=0 only after observing choice a makes a optimal; if b were chosen instead, redefining u(b)=1 and u(a)=0 would likewise make the choice optimal. Both retroactive functions match the observed choice, yet neither distinguishes any outcomes in advance, much less fear, interest, or commitment. Utility parameters with prior independent grounds that yield predictions capable of failure would present a different evidentiary situation.

BoundaryThis does not reject all utility models; it shows only that unconstrained retroactive filling-in lacks the discriminating power claimed here.

Teaching construction: when to discontinue the immune-system metaphorTeaching scenario

AssumptionsA design example for reviewing metaphors, not a biological mechanism or an actual team study.

Comparing a team's problem detection with recognizing anomalies may help ask about feedback channels. But members are not pathogens to be destroyed, and opinions are not diseases. The similarity concerns information recognition and response; differences concern human rights, meanings, and relations open to appeal. The risk of misuse is pathologizing dissent. If the metaphor supports suppression instead of helping distinguish facts, stop using it.

BoundaryWithout bridging evidence, an immune mechanism cannot be presented as a causal rule for human organizations.

An actual theoretical debate: Sen's distinction between consistent choice and reasonsDocumented case

On printed page 326 of his 1977 “Rational Fools,” Sen notes that consistent choice still does not resolve the issue of self-interest; pages 326–327 distinguish sympathy from commitment and discuss situations in which a choice happens to coincide with expected personal-welfare maximization without being made for that reason. This provides an original argumentative text distinguishing behavioral representation from identification of reasons.

SourceAmartya Sen，1977，Philosophy & Public Affairs 6(4)Original printed pp326–327 (scanned PDF pages 11–12), opening of page 326 and section IV, first 3 paragraphs of page 327Reading scope: Partly read

Scope and limitsI checked the relevant original-journal page images. This is neither an experiment nor proof of any particular person's motives, nor Sen's endorsement of all Xikari routes.

What does not follow

  • Failure does not cancel an evidenced R1, and success does not establish voluntariness; coerced actions can also have R2 effects.
  • R0 protection needs are not actual authority to protect; R1 does not generate an unlimited obligation to bear burdens.
  • These routes do not exhaust everyday love and care, and failure to satisfy a route does not negate personhood.
  • Broad utility permits more than narrow self-interest, but all-purpose retroactive fitting is not increased explanatory power.
  • Analogies with natural systems cannot authorize eliminating dissent, requisitioning labor, or depriving actors of rights.

Scope and open questions

The original pages of a theoretical debate directly cited by the book can be checked, serving as an actual intellectual-text case rather than invented behavioral observation.

  • No motives, voluntariness, or causal effects of actual undertakings have been identified.
  • This lesson has not compared utility models' out-of-sample explanatory power; the formal construction reveals only the problem of unconstrained retroactive filling-in.

16.15GOV-15 Knowledge Lineage and Source Transparency ​

In briefWhen borrowing others' concepts, the priority is not listing famous names but showing readers what was taken, what was changed, and how far the original author actually supports the claim. Renaming different methods with one common term does not mean their disagreements have been resolved.

For each concept that can be traced, record its intellectual affinities, specific source, version, what was retained, adapted, or abandoned, cross-cultural and cross-domain risks, and what the source can and cannot support. Acknowledging intellectual affinities does not weaken the framework. It reduces mystification and dogmatism.

Theoretical material cannot substitute for case evidence, a single case for a universal rule, an internal summary for original records, or an AI summary for a traceable source. The framework establishes interfaces for interoperability with other theories. It does not present itself as an overarching framework that absorbs them all.

Connections among bodies of knowledge should preserve where disagreements arise. Some theories estimate different outcomes. Some propose competing mechanisms for the same outcome. Some adopt different value premises. Common naming must not erase these differences. When retaining a method, state what it adds to the current task that can be distinguished. If a domain method already suffices, it should be possible to use only that method.

16.15Note
